index.content:
India 18th Century–Present
From the late Mughal order through Company sovereignty, Crown rule, and the political settlements of the twentieth century, India sat at the meeting of its own long civilizational continuum and the institutions, techniques, and ideas that arrived with European sea power. This knowledge base gathers sources that record that meeting as their authors saw it: law and education, press and railways, caste and Islam, missions and vernacular literature, and the smaller reverse current of Indian influence on the West.
Two Chatham House texts from the early 1940s sit on the shelf: O’Malley’s 1941 symposium and Whyte’s 1943 wartime Bird’s-Eye View. Beside them are B. R. Ambedkar’s Pakistan or the Partition of India (2nd ed. 1945; AMS 1975 reprint) and Maulana Abul Kalam Azad’s India Wins Freedom (complete version): the analytic case for Pakistan and a Congress president’s narrative of how freedom came with partition. Sir John Malcolm’s three-volume Life of Robert, Lord Clive (1836): Arcot, Plassey, the Diwani, and Clive’s last years. The earliest pamphlet on this shelf is Francis Russell’s 1793 Short History of the East India Company, written as the exclusive-trade term ran out. John Bruce’s official Annals (1810) are now complete in three volumes (1600–1707/8). James Mill’s History of British India, Wilson’s Madden set, is now complete in nine volumes: Mill through 1805 (vols I–VI) and Wilson 1805–1835 (vols VII–IX: 1813 charter; Hastings; Amherst/Burma/Bentinck and the 1833 charter). Beside them is Lucien Wolf’s 1921 Life of the First Marquess of Ripon, now complete in two volumes (to 1880; then the viceroyalty and last years to 1909). Sir Richard Temple’s India in 1880 (Murray, 3rd ed. 1881) surveys the empire at that same hinge — land, railways, famine, Russia, finance — from a Governor of Bombay and Finance Minister’s experience.

Sources
Scholarly surveys / Chatham House studies

Modern India and the West: A Study of the Interaction of Their Civilizations (O’Malley, ed., OUP for RIIA, 1941; lithographic reprint 1968) — Sixteen-chapter cooperative survey of Western impact on India since the sixteenth century (law, education, press, transport, economy, Christian ethic, Hinduism, caste, Islam, tribes, women, six vernacular literatures) and of Indian influence on the West, with O’Malley’s historical background, impact narrative, and closing general survey.
India: A Bird’s-Eye View (Whyte, RIIA / OUP 1943) — Short wartime briefing: historic India, the British Raj from the 1600 Company charter through the 1935 Act, Cripps and the 1942 crisis (Pakistan, Quit India), the Indian States and paramountcy, and India’s war effort, with parallel dates and statistical tables.

Partition / wartime political treatises

Pakistan or the Partition of India (Ambedkar, 2nd ed. 1945; AMS Press 1975) — Muslim case, Hindu objections, Hardayal and guessed Muslim parity alternatives, Turkey/Czechoslovakia lessons, communal malaise, and Part V on whether Pakistan must be, practical problems, and who can decide. Main text complete; appendices I–VII only in this EPUB.
India Wins Freedom (Azad / Humayun Kabir; Orient Blackswan complete version, sealed passages restored 1988) — Autobiographical narrative 1937–48: Congress ministries, wartime presidency, Cripps, Quit India, Ahmednagar, Simla, Cabinet Mission, Interim Government, Mountbatten, partition; Azad’s case that the Cabinet Mission Plan could have held India together.

Company records / Bruce

Annals of the Honorable East-India Company, Vol. I (Bruce, 1810) — 1600 through Charles II’s Restoration charter (1661): Portuguese and Dutch frame, first voyages, Surat, Roe, joint stocks, Courten and Interregnum.
Annals of the Honorable East-India Company, Vol. II (Bruce, 1810) — Chapter II, 1660–1 to 1688–9: Aurangzeb, Sivaji, Restoration charters, year-by-year to the Revolution.
Annals of the Honorable East-India Company, Vol. III (Bruce, 1810) — Chapter III, 1688–89 to the union of the London and English companies 1707–8. Completes the 1810 set.

Histories / Mill–Wilson

The History of British India, Vol. I (Mill; 4th ed. with notes by H. H. Wilson, Madden 1840) — Book I, British intercourse to Godolphin 1711; Book II, Of the Hindus (chronology, caste, government, laws, taxes, religion, manners). Vol. I of eight.
The History of British India, Vol. II (Mill/Wilson, 1840) — Book II continued (arts, literature, general reflections on Hindu civilization); Book III, The Mohammedans (Ghaznavids, Ghurids/Afghans, Mughal dynasty, comparison of Muslim and Hindu civilization). Vol. II of eight.
The History of British India, Vol. III (Mill/Wilson, 1840) — Book IV, exclusive Company 1708 to the Regulating Act 1773 (India House, Carnatic, Plassey, Lally, Meer Jafar/Mir Qasim, Diwani, Circars and Hyder, parliamentary reconstruction); Book V chs I–II, Hastings to Nuncomar. Vol. III of eight.
The History of British India, Vol. IV (Mill/Wilson, 1840) — Book V chs III–IX: Hastings after Nuncomar (revenue, Carnatic/Tanjore/Pigot, Hyder and Tippoo, Goddard and the Supreme Court, Benares, Oudh and the Begums, Dundas/Fox/Pitt). Completes Book V. Vol. IV of eight.
The History of British India, Vol. V (Mill/Wilson, 1840) — Book VI chs I–VI: Macpherson, Board of Control and Arcot debts, Cornwallis, Hastings impeachment and trial, third Mysore war, Permanent Settlement and its results. Vol. V of eight.
The History of British India, Vol. VI (Mill/Wilson, 1840) — Book VI chs VII–XIII: 1793 charter, Shore, Wellesley (Seringapatam, Oudh, Surat/Tanjore/Arcot), Bassein, Lake and Assye, Holkar, Cornwallis/Barlow. Completes Book VI and Mill’s narrative to 1805. Vol. VI of eight.
The History of British India, Vol. VII (Wilson continuation, Madden 1845) — Wilson Book I chs I–VIII: 1805–1813 (Barlow, Vellore, Minto, Travancore and the Madras officers, Java and Mauritius, dakoiti and revenue, 1813 charter). Vol. VII of the set.
The History of British India, Vol. VIII (Wilson continuation, Madden and Malcolm 1846) — Wilson Book II chs I–XII: 1813–1823, Marquis of Hastings (Nepal war, Kandy, Pindaris, last Maratha war, Central India, courts/revenue/press). Vol. VIII of nine.
The History of British India, Vol. IX (Wilson continuation, Madden 1848) — Wilson Book III / Volume III: 1823–1835, Adam and Amherst, first Burma war, Bhurtpore, Bentinck (suttee, thugs, English education), Coorg and Mysore, 1833 charter. Completes the nine-volume set.

Company pamphlets / 1793 charter

A Short History of the East India Company (Russell, 2nd ed., Sewell and Debrett 1793) — Origin and union of the old and new companies, India-House 3 per cent. annuities, purchased vs conquered forts, expenses of conquest, exclusive trade and the “monopoly” charge, foreign rivals, India and China commerce, the Company as sovereign and merchant, a regulated opening for private trade, Masulipatam and the Northern Circars, four-year sales, abridgment of the 1793 Act.

Contemporary lives / Viceroys

Life of the First Marquess of Ripon, Vol. I (Wolf, John Murray 1921) — Birth in Downing Street 1827 through Commons, War Office, Cabinet, Alabama claims, conversion to Rome, Gladstone’s Catholic Viceroy. Indian apprenticeship 1857–58. Vol. I of two.
Life of the First Marquess of Ripon, Vol. II (Wolf, John Murray 1921) — Viceroyalty 1880–84 (Afghanistan, Kandahar, Baring, local self-government, Vernacular Press Act, Ilbert Bill) and elder statesman to 1909. Completes the Life. Vol. II of two.

Contemporary surveys / Official India

India in 1880 (Temple, John Murray, 3rd ed. 1881) — Empire survey at Lytton/Ripon: Native States, land and revenues, canals and railways, famine, missions, army, Russia/Afghanistan, finance. Complete single volume.
Indian Musalmáns (W. Nassau Lees, Williams and Norgate 1871) — Three Times letters after Justice Norman’s assassination (loyalty, discontent, redress); Mayo’s 1871 Muslim-education resolution; critique of Macaulay’s 1835 Minute (printed in appendix). ZIP metadata says Hunter; text is Lees.

Contemporary lives / Company India

The Life of Robert, Lord Clive, Vol. I (Malcolm, John Murray 1836) — Clive’s family and boyhood, Carnatic wars and Arcot, return to England, Gheriah, Calcutta retaken, Chandernagore, Plassey, Mir Jafar, Northern Circars and the jaghir. Copy from the Great Britain 18th century wiki.
The Life of Robert, Lord Clive, Vol. II (Malcolm, 1836) — 1758–1767: Lally and Madras, the Dutch in Bengal, India House politics, second Bengal government, the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.
The Life of Robert, Lord Clive, Vol. III (Malcolm, 1836) — Last years 1766–1774: white mutiny of the Bengal army, salt monopoly, parliamentary inquiry, Clive’s death.

sources/ambedkar-pakistan-or-partition.title: B. R. Ambedkar — Pakistan or the Partition of India (2nd ed. / AMS 1975)
sources/ambedkar-pakistan-or-partition.content:
Pakistan or the Partition of India (Ambedkar, 2nd ed. / AMS 1975)
Dr. B. R. Ambedkar (Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar). Analytical wartime treatise on the Muslim League’s Lahore Resolution demand for Pakistan: Parts I–IV assemble the Muslim case, the Hindu case, alternatives if not Pakistan, and the communal “malaise”; Part V (added in the second edition) states the author’s own views. AMS Press, New York, 1975 reprint (ISBN-13 9780404548018). Local file: Anna’s Archive EPUB hash 3c0888173e68919472f3dd15c5ae163b.
Completeness
Main text of the second edition present; appendices incomplete in this EPUB.

Preface to the Second Edition (1 Jan. 1945, 22 Prithviraj Road, New Delhi); Prologue (28 Dec. 1940, Rajagrah, Dadar); Introduction; Parts I–V (Chapters I–XI, XIII–XV); Appendices I–VII (communal census tables).
Second-edition preface claims twenty-five appendices (first edition had eleven) plus an index. This EPUB’s appendix section stops at Appendix VII (N.-W.F.P. Muslim proportions by district). Maps mentioned in the Prologue are not recovered as images in the extract.
Chapter XII (National frustration) is listed in the main table of contents and named in the Part IV introduction as the third face of the malaise; this EPUB’s Part IV contents reprint and body chapter headers jump from XI to Part V. National-frustration material may be truncated or folded into the close of XI.
NCX / outline labels duplicate “CHAPTER VII” for what the body TOC correctly calls Chapter VIII (Muslim alternative to Pakistan). Body TOC is authoritative.
Closer: Appendix VII footnotes, then EPUB document outline stubs. No further narrative parts.

Summary
Written first as a report for the Independent Labour Party of Bombay after the League’s Lahore Resolution (March 1940); published so that students of Pakistan could assemble the data and decide for themselves. Ambedkar refuses to treat the demand as a passing political fever. He lays out the Muslim case (homogeneous Muslim-majority areas as national home; escape from Hindu-majority degradation after Congress ministries), tests the Hindu objections (break-up of unity; weakening of defences; failure to solve the communal question), examines Hindu and Muslim alternatives (Hardayal’s Sangathan/Shuddhi/conquest programme; a guessed Muslim parity constitution worse than the Communal Award), and draws lessons from the disruption of Turkey and of Czechoslovakia. Part IV turns from claims-adjustment to the reflex “malaise”: social stagnation on both sides, communal aggression, and national frustration of political destiny. Part V, new in the second edition after critics said he had described Pakistan without stating his own views, asks whether Pakistan must be; lists the practical problems of assets, boundaries, and population transfer; and drafts a procedure (Government of India (Preliminary Provisions) Act) for deciding by staged polls. Gandhi and Jinnah, he notes in the 1945 preface, cited the book in their talks. The book displeased both communities; Ambedkar treats that as evidence it is not a party production.
Source
Ambedkar, B. R. Pakistan or the Partition of India. Second edition (preface dated 1 January 1945). AMS Press, New York, 1975. ISBN 9780404548018. First edition commonly known as Thoughts on Pakistan. Local EPUB: Anna’s Archive 3c0888173e68919472f3dd15c5ae163b (wrapper also names Jagath Jayaprakash in the filename; title-page attribution is Ambedkar).
Full raw text extracted from EPUB XHTML (part0000–part0004 / part0003_split_*) at raw.txt (759,069 bytes; 9,758 lines; sha256 e06c523483d451cc148b0c0917e7da540450fde0c0eea282f5bc8ac0706b42a6). Clean digital text with footnote markers ([f.n]); tables split across short lines; some OCR-like typos inherited from the reprint (“tow aspects”, “he a remedy”).
Contents
Preface to the Second Edition (1 Jan. 1945)
Regrets the time the Pakistan question has consumed. Four differences from the first edition: misprints corrected; Part V added with the author’s own views; maps retained but appendices enlarged (11 → 25) and an index added. Notes that Gandhi and Jinnah cited the book in their recent talks. Calls the work more than an X.Y.Z. of Pakistan — an analytical presentation of Indian history and politics in their communal aspects, an “Indian Political What is What.” Displeased Hindus and Muslims for different reasons; takes that as evidence of independence of thought. Quotes Friedmann on states forcing recalcitrant national groups; contrasts senseless suppression with cases where diverse communities live in one state given the will. Thanks Prof. Manohar B. Chitnis (Khalsa College, Bombay) and K. V. Chitre for proofing and the index.
Prologue (28 Dec. 1940)
Origin of the treatise: after Lahore, the Independent Labour Party’s Executive Council appointed a committee (Ambedkar chairman; Donde, Joshi, Bhole, Jadhav, Chitre; Pradhan secretary) to study Pakistan. The published book is that report. Assembles data, appendices, and maps so the reader can conclude; invokes Carlyle’s warning against ostrich complacency. Thanks Tipnis (maps), Mody (typing), Kadrekar and Chitre (proofs).
Introduction
Pakistan is not political measles. Indian self-view has changed in twenty years; Toynbee’s 1915 “Sleeping Beauty” is awake and quarrelsome. Hindus and Muslims must decide the question themselves; Britain need not and will not coerce unity. Self-determination cuts both ways. Essence of Pakistan: opposition to one Central Government with supremacy over all India — two Centres instead. Silent Hindu premise that one Centre is settled is false: cultural antipathy among Hindu provinces; uneven financial burden of the Centre (central revenue ~Rs. 121 crore vs provincial ~Rs. 74 crore of ~Rs. 195 crore total). The scheme must be faced.
PART I — Muslim Case for Pakistan
Grounds claimed: ethnically more homogeneous administrative areas; those areas as separate States because Muslims are a nation wanting a home, and because Hindus use majority to degrade Muslims.
Chapter I — What does the League demand?
26 March 1940 Lahore Resolution quoted in full: geographic units demarcated where Muslims are a majority to form Independent States; minorities protected in both zones. Ambedkar parses what the League asks — not merely cultural safeguards inside one India, but territorial sovereignty for Muslim-majority zones (N.-W. and N.-E.).
Chapter II — A nation calling for a home
Tests whether Muslims constitute a nation. Race, language, and common country are insufficient (Renan: nation as living soul — shared past of glory and mourning, shared future ideal). Asks whether Hindus and Muslims share common historical antecedents as pride or sorrow; stresses forgetfulness and historical error as nation-making factors. Builds the two-nation claim from historical experience rather than ethnography alone.
Chapter III — Escape from degradation
Nationality as democratic warrant for a national state (Mill: boundaries of governments should coincide with nationalities). If grievances are required: constitutional safeguards failed. Fourteen points → Communal Award gave Muslims what they asked; Congress electoral victory in Hindu-majority provinces did not at first alarm Muslims; then League charges of tyranny under Congress ministries, refusal to treat the League as the sole Muslim voice, and cabinets without Muslim ministers commanding Muslim confidence. Instrument of Instructions on minority ministers; Governors declining to intervene. Congress replies (collective responsibility; good administration) miss the point: minorities refuse subject status even under a benevolent majority. A Hindu-composed body reflects Hindu mind.
PART II — Hindu Case against Pakistan
Three objections examined: break-up of unity; weakening of defences; failure to solve the communal problem.
Chapter IV — Break-up of Unity
Before mourning destroyed unity, ask whether it exists between Pakistan and Hindustan. Hsuan Tsang’s five Indies and eighty kingdoms; Afghanistan and the Punjab once within a Hindu political world. Warns against “historical sentiment” (conditions that once existed). Muslim invasions from the north-west (bin Qasim / Sind; Ghazni; Ghori; Taimur; Babar; Abdalli at Panipat 1761) as holy war as well as conquest — temple destruction, forced conversion, slavery — leaving a historical memory that cuts against a shared pride/sorrow nation. Unity under the British Raj is a different fact from ancient cultural unity.
Chapter V — Weakening of the Defences
How Pakistan would affect Hindustan’s defence under three heads: frontiers, resources, armed forces. No uniquely “scientific” frontier (Davies on the N.-W. Frontier; Forward Policy greater and lesser intents; Indus as base). Nations without natural boundaries can compensate. Comparative tables of area, population, and revenues for Pakistan provinces (N.-W.F.P., Punjab, Sind, Baluchistan) vs the rest. Armed-forces communal composition and the strategic weight of the north-west.
Chapter VI — Pakistan and communal peace
Communal Question in “lesser” and “greater” intent. Lesser: seats and electorates — separate electorates, weightage, statutory majority; Communal Award gave Muslims their claims; Hindu objections to weightage and statutory majority dissected; real grievance is a communal majority locked by separate electorates without easy alteration — majority has no divine right to rule. Greater intent: deliberate creation of nations within a nation; whether partition removes or relocates minority problems (Hindu minorities in Pakistan, Muslim minorities in Hindustan).
PART III — What if not Pakistan?
Chapter VII — Hindu alternative to Pakistan
Lala Hardayal’s 1925 political testament: Hindu Sangathan, Hindu Raj, Shuddhi of Muslims, conquest of Afghanistan and the frontier. Ambedkar doubts Hindu support: Hinduism not proselytising after caste crystallised (caste incompatible with conversion; convert needs a caste home); financial scale beyond Baniya habits of expenditure; Afghan/frontier conversion facilities. Other Hindu programmes of consolidation weighed and found wanting as substitutes for a territorial settlement.
Chapter VIII — Muslim alternative to Pakistan
(Body header in this EPUB mislabeled “CHAPTER VII”; TOC title is Chapter VIII.) Muslims disclose no alternative until bargaining day. Ambedkar’s guess: a constitution of 50% Muslim representation in legislatures, executives, civil service, and fighting forces; Muslim deputy where the Hindu holds the top post; 66% Muslim consent for boundary changes, action against Muslim countries, laws affecting Muslim culture/religion, and constitutional amendment; Urdu as national language; no cow-slaughter ban or anti-conversion law without that Muslim supermajority. Anchored in Hyderabad’s “functional” reform scheme as a hint of Muslim constitutional imagination; argued to be worse for Hindus than the Communal Award — hence Pakistan as the cleaner cut.
Chapter IX — Lessons from abroad
Turkey: rise from Central Asian displacement through Balkan and Arab empire; disruption from Egypt’s de facto break, Balkan Christian nationalities, Berlin, Young Turk revolution, Tripoli, Balkan League, Sevres, loss of Arab provinces — nationality inside the empire as the true solvent, not only European rapacity (Lane Poole; Eversley). Czechoslovakia: Trianon creation; twenty years; March 1939 destruction — not only German aggression on the Sudeten fringe but Slovak national consciousness denied by Czech–Slovak union assumptions. Moral for Hindus clinging to geographic unity against a nationality that will not will the common life.
PART IV — Pakistan and the Malaise
Hindu–Muslim problem has two aspects: adjustment of claims between two communities, and the reflex effects of separation and conflict on each. Malaise shows as (1) social stagnation, (2) communal aggression, (3) national frustration of political destiny. Will Pakistan remedy or aggravate it?
Chapter X — Social stagnation
Mother India publicised Hindu social evils and left the false impression that Muslims were free of them. Child-marriage tables (married females 0–15 per 1,000) for Hindus, Muslims, Jains, Sikhs, Christians across censuses from 1881. Parallel scrutiny of purdah, women’s status, caste-like stratifications among Muslims, and resistance to social reform when communal honour is at stake. Stagnation on both sides as product of communal siege mentality.
Chapter XI — Communal aggression
Aggression underlying Hindu attitude to Muslim and Muslim to Hindu. Social aggression and riot history; music before mosques; cow-slaughter as symbolic contest (Islamic law vs Hindu claim). Gangster methods in politics; Hindus no longer only passive. Rejection of Maha Sabha “strength” fantasies and of perpetual appeasement that buys off the aggressor by conniving at murder, rape, arson, loot. A settlement preferred to endless appeasement. (Chapter XII, National frustration — see Completeness.)
PART V — Epilogue (author’s views)
Chapter XIII — Must there be Pakistan?
Sceptic, nationalist, conservative, and old-world Indian will ask. Burden of proof on Muslims is heavy. Geographic concentration of Muslims does not erase India’s single geographic and long cultural unit. Communal antagonism exists — is there no will to live together? Canada (Brady on English/French) and South Africa (Brooks on Boer/British) as cases of deep difference under one polity where will and federal design hold. Loss of faith in Congress majority and unproven tyranny charges; two-nation theory as disintegration when the world seeks international organisation; “Hindu Raj” cry and its fallacies. Limitations on the Pakistan case stated before any affirmative.
Chapter XIV — The problems of Pakistan
Three practical problems: allocation of financial assets and liabilities; delimitation of areas; transfer of population. Plan of Pakistan vs principle of Pakistan are distinct; boundary specification is an essential preliminary. Self-determination: must be by the people (League and Maha Sabha both play loose with the idea); not a categorical imperative (O’Connor); may be cultural or territorial depending on facts on the ground.
Chapter XV — Who can decide?
Both sides irrational. Draft Government of India (Preliminary Provisions) Act: within six months, majority of Muslim members of N.-W.F.P., Punjab, Sind (and related) legislatures may trigger a poll; separate Muslim and non-Muslim polls on separation; if Muslims favour and non-Muslims oppose, a Boundary Commission; second poll on separation forthwith; then either two constitutions (Pakistan / Hindustan) or one; moratorium on fresh separation/incorporation motions; optional Council of India (President plus forty, half from each legislature) for delegated common subjects (railways, waterways, etc.), alterable by identical Acts. Procedure for decision without pretending the British will impose unity by force.
Appendices (I–VII in this EPUB)

Notes

Contemporary-lens reading: a 1940–45 brief that treats Pakistan as a justiciable constitutional problem — data, comparisons, and a draft statute — rather than as a slogan or a heresy.
Pairs with india-birds-eye-view (Whyte’s 1943 Cripps/Pakistan wartime briefing) and lees-indian-musalmans (1871 Muslim loyalty/education after Norman) for the long arc of Muslim–state questions; modern-india-and-the-west for the broader civilizational frame.
First edition title Thoughts on Pakistan often appears in bibliographies; this text is the enlarged second edition as reprinted by AMS in 1975.

sources/azad-india-wins-freedom.title: Maulana Abul Kalam Azad — India Wins Freedom (complete version)
sources/azad-india-wins-freedom.content:
India Wins Freedom (Azad, complete version)
Maulana Abul Kalam Azad (1888–1958; born Muhiyuddin Ahmad / Firoz Bakht). Autobiographical narrative of the decade of transfer of power, dictated in conversation to Humayun Kabir and approved by Azad sentence by sentence. Dedicated to Jawaharlal Nehru, “friend and comrade.” Orient Blackswan complete version (court-released 1988 text; this EPUB Orient Blackswan 2018 / e-edition lineage from 2011). Local file: Anna’s Archive EPUB hash 44bc93b0db4856d43d1b4d2b783e8424.
Completeness
Complete as the published complete-version single volume.

Front matter: About the author; title (the complete version); copyright; dedication; Publishers’ Note (Oct. 1988); Contents; Preface to the 1959 edition (Kabir, 15 Mar. 1958); Prospectus (planned first-volume synopsis to 1937).
Body: sixteen chapters (Congress in Office through Divided India) + Epilogue.
Appendixes 1–5: Kabir’s editor’s note on sealed passages; Cripps Draft Declaration (29 Mar. 1942); correspondence with Cripps; further documents through the Mountbatten / 3 June plan materials (Punjab and Bengal Muslim-majority districts by 1941 census).
Restored passages marked with asterisks at beginning and end, per Publishers’ Note. Closer: end of Appendix 5 district lists. Planned Vol. I (to 1937) and Vol. III (after 1948) were never written.

Summary
Azad’s reading of how India won freedom and lost unity. Kabir spent evenings with him from about 1956; drafted in English; Azad revised repeatedly and, for the 1959 book, withheld roughly thirty pages of personal judgements under seal until thirty years after his death. The 1988 complete edition, ordered released by the Delhi High Court from the National Library and National Archives deposits, restores those passages (and Kabir’s earlier softennings) throughout the text. The narrative runs from the 1937 provincial elections and Congress office, through wartime Congress presidency, the Cripps Mission, Quit India and Ahmednagar Fort jail, the Simla Conference, the 1945–46 elections, the Cabinet Mission Plan (which Azad saw as the federal solution that could have held India together), the Interim Government, Mountbatten’s arrival, and partition. Azad’s through-line: partition was avoidable; Patel fell first for Mountbatten’s scheme; Nehru’s succession as Congress president after Azad was “perhaps the greatest blunder” of Azad’s political life; geography made a consolidated Muslim state impossible; Pakistan solved no communal problem and weakened Muslims on both sides of the new border.
Source
Azad, Maulana Abul Kalam. India Wins Freedom: the complete version. Orient Blackswan Private Limited. Text adapted from the original complete edition published by Orient Blackswan / Orient Longman in 1988 (Publishers’ Note, October 1988); © 1959; eISBN 978 81 250 4482 6; e-edition first published 2011; this Anna’s Archive EPUB wrapper 2018, ISBN-13 9788125005148, hash 44bc93b0db4856d43d1b4d2b783e8424. Narrative composed in English under Azad’s direction by Humayun Kabir; not Azad’s own Urdu prose.
Full raw text extracted from EPUB XHTML (spine order) at raw.txt (598,149 bytes; 2,385 lines; sha256 96e9da7b52c4b61595998e0195e653f4910769207bb08671e5e316161f320e7b). Clean digital text; running header “India Wins Freedom”; asterisk-bounded restored passages; occasional typos inherited from the edition.
Contents
About the author / front matter
Sketch of Azad: Mecca birth 1888; Al Hilal (Calcutta, 1912); opposition to Aligarh aloofness from Congress; Khilafat and Congress presidency; works including Tarjuman-ul-Quran. Kabir’s academic and political résumé as amanuensis. Dedication to Nehru.
Publishers’ Note (October 1988)
Manuscript handed over September 1958 after Azad’s death; fuller sealed text promised for 22 February 1988 (thirtieth death anniversary). Hand-over delayed by litigation; Justice B. N. Kirpal (Delhi High Court, 29 Sept. 1988) ordered identical National Library / National Archives copies released to Orient Longman for reproduction without alteration. “Additional matter” not a discrete thirty pages but scattered omissions and Kabir editorial softenings throughout. Asterisks mark major restorations. Prospectus and original appendixes retained.
Preface to the 1959 Edition (Humayun Kabir, 15 Mar. 1958)
Azad reluctant (health; dislike of personal talk); persuaded that a principal actor in the transfer of power owed a record to posterity. Method: evening conversations; English drafts; joint revision; completed draft September 1957; ~thirty pages of personal incidents sealed for National Library and National Archives; abridged draft November 1957; final approval Republic Day 1958. Book meant for November 1958 (seventieth birthday); Azad died first. Prospectus retained as synopsis of the never-written first volume (to 1937); a third volume after 1948 also intended. Royalties partly to Indian Council for Cultural Relations for essay prizes on Islam/Hinduism by citizens of India or Pakistan under thirty. Kabir records disagreements with some judgements but refuses to colour the narrative.
Prospectus (of the planned first volume)
Family from Herat in Babar’s days; Agra then Delhi; scholarly Mughal service (Jamaluddin under Akbar; Munawaruddin as Rukn-ul Mudarassin). Father Khairuddin to Mecca before/around 1857; Azad born Mecca 1888; family to Calcutta 1890. Traditional Arabic/Persian education; crisis of faith after reading Sir Syed; Curzon and the Partition of Bengal; contact with Shyam Sunder Chakravarty and Hindu-middle-class revolutionary groups then actively anti-Muslim. Stops as the gate into the 1937–48 narrative that fills this volume.
1 — Congress in Office
1937 elections under provincial autonomy: Congress absolute majority in five major provinces. Early reluctance to contest or take office under the 1935 Act; interim non-Congress ministries; then office as a trial of the organisation. Restored: Nariman denied Bombay leadership to satisfy Patel’s communal preferences; Parsee enquiry whitewash; Syed Mahmud passed over for Bihar chief ministership despite being the province’s top Congressman and AICC General Secretary. Congress ideals not lived up to. Glance back to C. R. Das’s practical federal foresight and the 1921 Prince of Wales boycott.
2 — War in Europe
Munich and Congress dissociation from British foreign policy that aided Fascist powers. Gandhiji’s deepening gloom and wish that India declare non-participation; Azad differs — Europe’s war is also India’s stake once Fascism threatens. Provincial Congress ministries still in office against this sombre backdrop.
3 — I Become Congress President
War breaks 3 September 1939; Poland falls. Azad elected Congress president unopposed in substance. Congress resolution on the war: no free India’s war without Indian consent; British policy in India unchanged. Expectancy and fear in India; presidential burden in a transformed international scene.
4 — A Chinese Interlude
Roosevelt’s concern for India’s voluntary war participation. Nehru’s pre-war visit to Chiang Kai-shek; Chiang and Madame arrive Delhi 9 February 1942; talks with Congress leaders. Bridge chapter into the spring of the Cripps Mission.
5 — The Cripps Mission
Deepening war crisis; expectation of a British shift. Stafford Cripps’s aide-mémoire and defence formula; Azad will not commit on a hypothetical. Draft Declaration (Dominion union; provincial non-accession / secession analogue; wartime defence reserved to H.M.G.). Congress concentration on present defence responsibility vs vague “National Government” that remains the Viceroy’s Executive Council. Failure of the Mission.
6 — Uneasy Interval
Disappointment and anger after Cripps. Azad reports to AICC: British attitude unhelpful since war’s outbreak; Congress had sought effective Indian responsibility for defence. Climate that feeds the Quit India resolution.
7 — Quit India
Working Committee resolution creates an electric atmosphere; wait for Government reaction; foreign press at Wardha. After passage, Mahadev Desai and Mira Ben. Arrests follow; the organisation goes into the wilderness of 1942–45.
8 — Ahmednagar Fort Jail
Nine Working Committee members with Azad: Nehru, Patel, Asaf Ali, etc. Military-barrack detention; iron platters; place of detention kept secret (futile). Jail routines, reading, internal debates; the long pause while the war turns.
9 — The Simla Conference
American pressure for an Indian settlement after 1942 arrests; wartime improvement in Europe renews it. Wavell’s Simla Conference: attempt at a reconstituted Executive Council; League–Congress deadlock over parity and League claim to all Muslim seats. Failure that sets up the post-war elections.
10 — General Elections
Doctors send Azad to Kashmir (Gulmarg). Viceroy announces general elections for the coming winter. Atom bombs on Japan — Azad still convinced there was no justification. Electoral contest that strengthens both Congress and League mandates for the Cabinet Mission round.
11 — The British Cabinet Mission
February 1946: a transformed India. Pethick-Lawrence’s announcement (17 Feb.); Attlee’s 15 March Commons speech (faults on both sides; no precedent in Indo-British relations). Mission arrives 23 March. Azad’s core constitutional conclusion: India must be federal; defence, communications, and foreign affairs only workable on an all-India basis. The Cabinet Mission Plan as the frame that could reconcile League fears with Indian unity — the solution he never abandons.
12 — Prelude to Partition
Political and communal problems seemed solved; Congress needs a new president. Restored: Azad’s decision not to continue, and his support of Nehru over Patel, as “perhaps the greatest blunder of my political life” — convinced that Patel as president would have held the Cabinet Mission Plan. AICC approval of the Plan; Nehru takes the chair; subsequent glosses and League withdrawal begin the unravelling.
13 — Interim Government
Parliamentary Committee forms the Interim Government. Azad presses for a Parsee seat (as at Simla); economist as first Indian Finance Member. League rage at being left out, then entry; Finance in League hands becomes a lever that later paralyses the Centre. Path into the Mountbatten months.
14 — The Mountbatten Mission
Mountbatten sworn 24 March 1947; tells Azad at once that Britain will transfer power. Communal deterioration (Calcutta, Noakhali, Bihar, Bombay, Punjab); European services losing heart; Congress–League deadlock inside the Executive Council. Central claim: Patel first fell for Mountbatten’s partition idea; Mountbatten then worked on Nehru; Pakistan had been for Jinnah in part a bargaining counter. Assam pressure despite non-Muslim majority. Administration lax as passions mount.
15 — The End of a Dream
Lingering hope Labour would not discard the Cabinet Mission Plan. Mountbatten’s plan published; first open discard of the Mission Plan for partition. Commonwealth question; Churchill’s hostility to the Mission Plan. Working Committee 3 June; Frontier / Khudai Khidmatgars; Gandhiji’s surprising conversion to the Mountbatten Plan; Khan brothers, Pakhtoonistan, and the Frontier referendum. Dream of united India ends.
16 — Divided India
14–15 August 1947: Mountbatten inaugurates Pakistan; India free at midnight — and wakes to massacre. Ten-year retrospect: Congress leaders had not accepted partition with conviction; Patel the greatest Congress supporter of it, yet even he did not think it best. 14 August as mourning for Hindus and Sikhs; Muslim League leaders left in India claim Jinnah deceived them — they had not grasped Pakistan’s implications. Hostage-and-reprisal doctrine applied in Delhi. Freedom with tragedy.
Epilogue
Gandhi’s assassination; failure of Delhi police/CID after the prior bomb; restored passage on Patel’s indifference during Gandhi’s fast for Muslim security and its effect on local officials. Jayaprakash Narayan and P. C. Ghosh hold the Home Minister responsible; Patel rallies the Congress Parliamentary Party. Sweets distributed in Gwalior and Jaipur; brief isolation of Hindu Mahasabha / RSS; Godse trial; Patel’s later heart attack. Freedom gained, unity lost. Pakistan’s leadership drawn from UP/Bihar/Bombay without local roots; elections postponed; Muslims weakened on both sides (45 million left in India). Partition constitutionalised enmity; defence budgets explode (Wavell’s ~100 crore vs post-partition ~250 crore for India, ~100+ for Pakistan). Geography against a consolidated Muslim state; East and West Pakistan already divergent; Islam alone has not held Muslim countries together after the first generations. Die cast: friendship between India and Pakistan the only sane course. History to judge whether partition was inevitable or avoidable — Azad’s vote is for the Cabinet Mission alternative.
Appendixes

Notes

Contemporary-lens reading: a principal Congress Muslim’s near-contemporary brief on why the Cabinet Mission federal formula was preferable to Mountbatten partition — written for posterity with sealed candour restored in 1988.
Pairs with ambedkar-pakistan-or-partition (analytic case for/against Pakistan, 1940–45) and india-birds-eye-view (Whyte’s 1943 Cripps/Quit India briefing) for the wartime–partition shelf.
Dictated English under Kabir is the authorised text Azad approved; it is not a translation of an Urdu original of this book.

sources/bruce-annals-eic-vol1.title: John Bruce — Annals of the Honorable East-India Company, Vol. I (1810)
sources/bruce-annals-eic-vol1.content:
Annals of the Honorable East-India Company, Vol. I (Bruce, 1810)
John Bruce, M.P., F.R.S., Keeper of His Majesty’s State Papers and Historiographer to the East-India Company. Volume I of a three-volume official chronicle from the 1600 charter to the union of 1707–8: this volume is the Restoration horizon (charter of Charles II, 1661).
Completeness
This file is a complete Volume I. It is not the complete Annals.

Title-page: VOL. I. 1600 to the union 1707–8 as the work’s full span; this volume’s Chapter I is 1600–1661.
Last printed leaf: END OF VOL. I (twice in the Google scan), then Cox, Son, and Baylis, then Stanford Auxiliary Library date-due slip.
593 PDF pages; extract runs out at that closer. No Volume II or III title-pages, no 1661–1708 narrative.
The finished work (1810) is three volumes. Vols II–III (Restoration through the Godolphin union of the London and English companies) are missing from the local PDF.

Google Books reproduction (Stanford copy). OCR noisy (broken words, “Queeris” for Queen’s, “F.ND OF VOL.”). Substance of Vol. I is present from preface through the closer.
Summary
Printed by authority of the Court of Directors. Preface: the Annals are a subordinate branch of England’s political and commercial history, drawn from the State-Paper Office and the Company’s Indian Register Office, submitted to Directors, Proprietors, the Legislature, and the Public. The early charters and exclusive privileges are to be useful when those privileges come again before Parliament.
Introduction: ancient mixed land-and-sea trade to the Mediterranean; Vasco da Gama 1497; Portuguese seats on the Indian coasts; union of the Spanish and Portuguese crowns as the source of Portuguese fall in the East; Dutch companies to the Truce of Antwerp (1609), oppressions of English and Portuguese, measures after 1621 and after Münster 1648; sketch of native powers within the London Company’s limits; England’s relations with maritime states from Elizabeth’s charter (1600) through James I, Charles I, and the Interregnum to the Restoration (1660).
Chapter I (the volume’s body): resources of sixteenth-century monarchies; Russia and Levant companies as the school of the direct East-Indian trade; Drake and Cavendish; merchants’ memorial 1589; Raymond 1591; Adams and Bromfield China project 1596; London Adventurers’ contract 1599; Foulke Grevil; charter 31 December 1600; first experimental voyages; Michelborne’s licence as first violation; James’s charter 31 May 1609; Surat licences and Jahangir’s farmans; First Joint Stock 1612–13; Japan; Swally and the Portuguese; Sir Thomas Roe 1614–15; Polaroon; then a regular year-by-year review from 1617–18 (Second Joint Stock, Dutch factory at Surat, Shirley in Persia) through Dutch–English disputes, Amboyna, Courten’s Association, Assada merchants, Merchant Adventurers, Civil War and Interregnum stocks, to the Restoration of privileges by Charles II’s charter (1661). Closer: interloping associations interrupt or exclude the London Company from purchased ports, then go bankrupt or merge into the joint stock; neither monarchy nor Interregnum questioned the Company’s “dead stock” of forts, factories, and native privileges.
Source
Bruce, John. Annals of the Honorable East-India Company, from the Establishment by the Charter of Queen Elizabeth, 1600, to the Union of the London and English East-India Companies, 1707-8. Vol. I. London: Cox, Son, and Baylis for Black, Parry, and Kingsbury, 1810. Entered at Stationers’ Hall. Stanford University Libraries digitization (Google Books PDF converter). Local file: Anna’s Archive PDF, 26 MB, 593 pages.

Contents
Dedication
To the Court of Directors of the United Company of Merchants of England trading to the East-Indies.
Preface
Evidence from State Papers and the Indian Register Office; rights under charters; usefulness when exclusive privileges again come before the legislature.
Introduction
Ancient and modern commercial intercourse Europe–East Indies; Portuguese discoveries and power before and after the Spanish union; Dutch rise, Antwerp 1609, post-1621 exclusion policy, Münster 1648; native powers in the Company’s limits; England and the maritime states 1600–1660 (Elizabeth, James I, Charles I, Interregnum).
Chapter I — Annals of the London East-India Company, 1600–1661
Printed contents of the chapter (compressed): Russia and Levant companies; 1589 memorial; Raymond; 1599 Adventurers; Elizabeth’s charter 31 Dec. 1600; first voyages; Michelborne; James’s charter 31 May 1609; Surat and Jahangir; First Joint Stock 1612–13; Roe; Polaroon; then seasonal headings from 1617–18 onward (Second Joint Stock; Dutch at Surat; Persia; Bantam; 1618–19 Dutch memorial and Roe–Churrum treaty; Mocha; 1619–20 commissioners on Spice Island disputes; later seasons through Courten, Civil War, Interregnum joint stocks, Cromwell, to Charles II 1661).
The extract’s year-tags in the body include (among others) 1617–18, 1618–19, 1619–20, 1621–22, 1623–24, 1624–25, 1625–26, 1628–29, 1631–32, 1634–35, 1636–37, 1638–39, 1639–40, 1642–43, 1645–46, 1648–49, 1650–51, 1652, 1653–54, 1654–55, 1655, 1656, 1657–58, 1658–59.

Needs vols II and III before the Annals can be treated as the full 1600–1708 record Bruce advertised. sources/bruce-annals-eic-vol2.content:
Annals of the Honorable East-India Company, Vol. II (Bruce, 1810)
Which part: Volume II — Chapter II — Restoration (1660–1) to the Revolution (1688–9).
John Bruce, M.P., F.R.S., Keeper of the State Papers and Historiographer to the Company. Second volume of the three-volume official chronicle. Title-page OCR: “völ. ii.” Running headers VOL. II. The body is a single Chapter II.
Completeness
This file is a complete Volume II. The three-volume Annals are still incomplete.





















PieceStatusVol. I (1600–1661)Already extracted: bruce-annals-eic-vol1Vol. II (1660–1 to 1688–9)This PDF — 747 pages, closer ENIO OF VOL. II (OCR for END OF VOL. II), Cox, Son, and Baylis, Stanford date-due slipVol. III (Revolution to the 1707–8 union)Missing
No Volume III title-page in this scan. Google Books / Stanford copy, same series as Vol. I.
Summary
Chapter heading: Review of the Annals of the London East-India Company, from the Restoration of their Privileges by King Charles II., in 1660-1, to the Revolution, 1688-9.
Introduction compares the first period (foundation to Restoration: Dutch rival, licensed interlopers, yet a preserved foreign trade) with this second period, when the Company keeps stations while the English constitution and European maritime relations are “frequently unhinged,” now favoured by the Crown that restored the charter. Sketches: England under Charles II and James II (Interregnum treaties kept in view); native powers in the peninsula in Aurangzeb’s reign — accession and consolidation; conquest of the Deccan; origin and progress of Sivaji; persecution of Hindus and their union against Mogul government; death of Sivaji, Sambhaji, Bijapur and Golconda, Rajaram/“Sahogee” as chief of the Hindu confederacy, Tanjore; third object, enlargement of Mogul resources.
The annalistic body then runs season by season from 1660–61 / 1661–62 through 1688–89 (headers in the extract include 1661–62 … 1687–88, 1688–89). Closer (Results): at the Revolution the Court of Committees kept commercial caution, had not been parties to domestic changes of government, directed views to trade and settlements, then united in supporting the “free constitution” at home and abroad. Numbered result XI on naval force in the Indian seas, superior to native princes and equal to European armaments in a European war.
Source
Bruce, John. Annals of the Honorable East-India Company … 1600 … 1707-8. Vol. II. London: Cox, Son, and Baylis for Black, Parry, and Kingsbury, 1810. Stanford Auxiliary Library digitization (Google Books PDF converter). Local file: Anna’s Archive PDF hash 575ec9a5b31ef2c97f390dba134f144d, 95 MB, 747 pages. Title / Chapter II heading
Work-span still advertised as 1600–1707/8; this volume is the Restoration-to-Revolution slice.
Introduction to Chapter II
England 1660–1688/9 (Charles II, James II). Aurangzeb: consolidation, Deccan, Sivaji and Sambhaji, Bijapur, Golconda, Tanjore, resources of the empire.
Annals, 1660–1 to 1688–9
Year/season review of London Company domestic and foreign transactions (Surat, Fort St George, Bengal, Bombay, factories) through the Revolution. Closing “Results,” including naval force in the Indian seas and the Directors’ conduct at 1688–89.

sources/india-birds-eye-view.title: Sir Frederick Whyte — India: A Bird's-Eye View (1943)
sources/india-birds-eye-view.content:
India: A Bird’s-Eye View (Whyte, 1943)
A short wartime Chatham House pamphlet by Sir Frederick Whyte, K.C.S.I., giving a five-chapter “bird’s-eye” of historic India, the British Raj, the political crisis of 1942 (Cripps Mission, Pakistan, Congress “Quit India”), the Indian States under paramountcy, and India’s part in the Second World War, closed by a table of parallel dates and statistical tables.
Summary
Printed in the United States for the Royal Institute of International Affairs (RIIA disclaimer: the Institute expresses no opinion; opinions are the author’s). Title-page date 1943; Rutgers copy stamped 12-15-43. Companion in this wiki to the larger 1941 Chatham House symposium Modern India and the West (O’Malley): Whyte is the short contemporary briefing while O’Malley is the specialist survey.
Whyte opens by placing India apart even from the rest of Asia: a sub-continent of Himalaya, Indo-Gangetic plain, and Deccan; monsoon and irrigation; 1941 census “not far short of 400 millions”; a land of peasants near the margin of subsistence; Hinduism as the social frame that left politics a modern Western growth. The Raj chapter runs from Elizabeth’s East India Company charter (31 December 1600), paired with Charles I’s Massachusetts company, through Bombay (1661/1669), Company-to-Crown 1858, Queen’s Proclamation, English education and Congress, Tilak and Gandhi, 1917 Declaration, 1919 Act and Statutory Commission, Round Table Conference and federal hope, to the 1935 Act and the outbreak of war with India automatically at war when the King was at war.
Chapter III treats the Cripps Mission of early 1942 as the outstanding political event of that spring: not a barren failure, Whyte argues, but a new climate and an accelerated movement along the line of 1917. Pakistan (the “istan” coinage), League resolutions, Atlantic Charter Point 3, the Draft Declaration (union, secession analogue, treaty), Sikh and Liberal responses, Rajagopalachari, and Congress rejection (1 May) through the Bombay “Quit India” resolution (August 1942) occupy the narrative. Chapter IV sizes the States (712,000 sq. miles; 92 million people; 39 per cent of area, 23 per cent of population; 21-gun salute group) and the doctrine of paramountcy after the Mutiny. Chapter V turns to the Indian Army, industry, and the wartime reduction of India’s sterling debt. Appendices: parallel dates from Vasco da Gama / Akbar / Vijayanagar 1565 / Company 1600 onward; statistical tables of area, population, cities, religions, languages, communities, occupation, factories, metals, railways, cotton mills, and trade 1937–40; maps of political divisions and communications (present in the scan as listed, not as recovered images in this extract).
Source
Whyte, Sir Frederick, K.C.S.I. India: A Bird’s-Eye View. London: The Royal Institute of International Affairs; New York, Toronto, Bombay, Melbourne, Cape Town: Oxford University Press, 1943. Call mark on this copy DS436 W624. OCLC 6500297 (Anna’s Archive wrapper dated 1942; printed title-page 1943). Rutgers / New Jersey College for Women copy.
Full raw text concatenated from 84 per-page OCR files in the local ZIP (RUTGERS_39030022325403_00000001.txt … _00000084.txt) at raw.txt (182,808 bytes; 4,277 lines; sha256 c9f78e2ae99169415238fc43f2e4f44d241b3f4d7e81f5b1cdb9c864a877d954). OCR medium: broken hyphenation, running headers, occasional Japanese/garbled bookplate on the library leaf, “Bird’s-Eve” for “Eye” on the cover transcription. Page markers in the extract are ZIP sequence numbers, not always identical to printed pagination (printed contents: I p. 5, II p. 13, III p. 30, IV p. 45, V p. 53, Appendix I p. 61, Appendix II p. 68).
Contents
Printed contents: I Historic India; II The British Raj; III The Crisis of 1942; IV The Indian States; V India in the War; Appendix I Table of Parallel Dates; Appendix II Statistical Tables; Maps (India: Political Divisions; India: Communications).
I — Historic India
“There is no country in the world which presents a picture of greater variety than India.” Contrast with the West; India as an element the European must unclothe his mind to enter; Maya and reversed values. Three regions; monsoon (Upper Sind 3.6 inches vs Cherrapunji 400); irrigation and railways said almost to have driven famine out. 1941 census approaching 400 million; density from Cochin 4,000 per sq. mile to Baluchistan 6.5; two-thirds of the people on one-quarter of the land. Peasants; James VI’s “beggar’s mantle fringed with gold”; Gandhi and the charkha; Hinduism, illiteracy, moneylender debt, and the cow as obstacles to agricultural reform. Literacy 9.3 per cent Bengal to 4.2 per cent NWFP. About 70 per cent Hindu, 22 per cent Mohammedan, plus Christians, Sikhs, Jains, Parsees, Jews. Cohesion by Hinduism (belief, custom, law, ritual) rather than monarchy or secular law; political life a modern Western growth. Islam as successive conquest culminating in the Mogul Empire; a more radical distinction from Hinduism than Catholic/Protestant in Europe.
II — The British Raj
Opens 31 December 1600, Elizabeth’s East India Company charter; 1628 Charles I’s Massachusetts company as the twin seed of empire East and West, now converging in the twentieth century (Statute of Westminster, Cripps). Bombay from Catherine of Braganza (1661) transferred to the Company (1669); charters Cromwell 1657, Charles II 1661, Anne 1709; Company as “Sovereign Corporation.” Reform Act 1832 Parliament and James Mill’s caution (“engraft on despotism the natural fruits of liberty”). Transfer to the Crown; John Company’s last instructions on the civil and military services. Drain/interest argument answered by exchange of British manufactures and Indian produce. Social reform against infanticide, human sacrifice, child marriage, temple prostitution, widow remarriage ban. Queen’s Proclamation: good government, justice, toleration, progress, and Indian employment — no word of democracy or responsibility except to Crown and Imperial Parliament. Tilak (force) and Gandhi (opposite tactics) as two campaigns from Hindu revival; English education as the vehicle of political awakening; National Congress. First World War Indian troops and infant industry; 1917 Declaration; 1919 Act and ten-year Statutory Commission; Round Table Conference and proposed Federal Union of British India and the States; Irwin/Halifax 1931; war outbreak with Congress refusing co-operation because India was automatically at war.
III — The Crisis of 1942
“The Cripps Mission to India was the outstanding political event of the early spring of 1942.” Whyte refuses “barren failure”: new climate; Declaration as heir of 1917, not a radical departure. Pakistan etymology (Punjab, Afghan Frontier, Kashmir + istan); League’s reaffirmation of Pakistan and disapproval of a constitution based on India’s economic and political unity. Atlantic Charter Point 3 (“right of all peoples to choose the form of Government”). Draft Declaration: new constitution, possible separate union of same full status, treaty with H.M. Government. Sikhs: “resist by all possible means the separation of the Punjab from the All-India Union.” Sapru and Jayakar on the Defence portfolio. All-India Congress Committee rejects British proposals 1 May; Rajagopalachari’s Madras friends urge acknowledging the League claim and talking to Jinnah. Working Committee to All-India Committee in Bombay (7 August): “Quit India”; Labour, Depressed Classes, M. N. Roy’s Left. Whyte: India as a whole in the war; Congress had failed to gauge prevailing sentiment; Sir Ramaswami Mudaliar on Pacific War Council and War Cabinet.
IV — The Indian States
Five 21-gun States named: Baroda, Gwalior, Hyderabad, Kashmir, Mysore. 712,000 square miles vs British India’s one million; 92 million people vs 296 million (39 per cent of area, 23 per cent of population). Paramountcy: disputes settled by British officers’ rules or orders, not agreements; Patiala–Nabha arbitration by the Viceroy. Pre-Mutiny isolation of States; Mutiny as change of mind after Company unrest. Post-1858 suzerainty “eagerly acknowledged by the Chiefs”; Hyderabad sanad 1862, succession invalid unless recognized by the King-Emperor. Ideal of provinces and states working out destinies and combining for imperial purposes.
V — India in the War
Martial spirit of the Army in India (British and Indian) as the Raj’s claim to have enlisted communities in a common purpose. Economic shift: commerce before industry; heavy industry in the wake of railways; pre-1914 iron and steel. Wartime finance: India’s sterling obligations reduced (figure given for 1941–42, £90,000,000, “will soon be reduced to zero”); British investment in railways, irrigation, and public works becoming Indian-owned free of interest encumbrance.
Appendix I — Table of Parallel Dates
Facing columns of general / Indian dates. Sample openings in the extract: 1497–8 voyage; 1556–1605 Akbar; 1565 fall of Vijayanagar; 1600 East India Company; 1602 Dutch EIC; 1604 French EIC; 1634 English trade throughout Mogul dominions; 1639 Madras / Fort St George.
Appendix II — Statistical Tables
As listed in contents: total area; total population; ten principal cities; population by religions; main languages; communities; occupation; factories in British India; principal metallurgical products; railway mileage; progress of cotton mill industry; distribution of Indian trade (merchandise); principal imports 1937–40; principal exports of Indian merchandise 1937–40.
Notes for later extraction
Pair with modern-india-and-the-west for 1941–43 Chatham House India. Natural first filings: Cripps Mission 1942, Pakistan coinage, Quit India, Indian States/paramountcy, 1600 Company charter. Entity/event pages await Proceed.

sources/lees-indian-musalmans.title: W. Nassau Lees — Indian Musalmáns (1871)
sources/lees-indian-musalmans.content:
Indian Musalmáns (Nassau Lees, 1871)
W. Nassau Lees (Fellow of Calcutta University; LL.D. Dublin; Ph.D. Berlin; late Principal of the Mohammadan College of Calcutta). Williams and Norgate, London and Edinburgh, 1871. Michigan copy 39015030535176.

Completeness
Complete as a single pamphlet-volume.

Title-page lists the three Times letters, Prince Consort article, four Calcutta Englishman education articles (1866), and Macaulay’s Minute in an appendix. 126 OCR leaves.
Closer: end of Macaulay’s Minute (“THE END”), then a short letter from Garcin de Tassy (Times, Paris, 17 Nov.) clarifying Lees’s position. No further parts.

Summary
Written in the weeks after the stabbing of Mr Justice Norman in Calcutta. Lees defends the loyalty of the great body of Indian Muslims, separates the assassin from the community, then argues that Muslim discontent is real and remediable: Permanent Settlement and resumptions, English-only higher education after Macaulay, and the eclipse of the Calcutta Mohammadan College. He reprints Mayo’s August 1871 Home Department resolution on Mohammadan education, presses for Arabic/Persian and vernaculars beside English, and prints Macaulay’s February 1835 Minute so readers can judge the “Battle of the Orientalists and the Anglicists” themselves.
Source
Lees, W. Nassau. Indian Musalmáns: Being Three Letters Reprinted from the “Times,” with an Article on the late Prince Consort, and Four Articles on Education, Reprinted from the “Calcutta Englishman.” With an Appendix containing Lord Macaulay’s Minute. Williams and Norgate, 14 Henrietta Street, Covent Garden, London; and 20 South Frederick Street, Edinburgh. 1871. OCLC on the ZIP points at Hunter; content is Lees. Local file: Anna’s Archive ZIP hash 43677ea7bfc580c9e19d33c4a443a143.
Full raw text concatenated at raw.txt (161,261 bytes; 3,882 lines; sha256 0cc9f63da4189b129a68d0a97060a8fd5f615ab50ce9a7a3c44d8a0eed13ccf5). OCR medium.
Contents
Advertisement (Athenæum, 10 Nov. 1871)
Lees denies wanting a return to Warren Hastings’s Muslim monopoly of civil office or exclusive Oriental subsidies. He wants English, Sanskrit, Arabic, Persian, and the vernaculars each in place. Prints Lord Mayo’s Resolution (Simla, August 1871, Home Department Education): Muslims under-use government schools except perhaps NWP and Punjab; encourage Arabic and Persian; vernacular secondary/higher education; Muslim English teachers; grants-in-aid for Muslim schools; vernacular literature; consult universities and Lahore. Lees’s only objection: legislate for Muslim education as part of educating all the peoples of the Indian Empire, not Muslims alone.
Letter I — To the Editor of the Times (14 Oct. 1871)
On Norman’s assassination. Personal tribute: Norman’s kindness to Calcutta Muslims makes personal animosity almost impossible; he died for unflinching discharge of office. Rejects general charges of Muslim disloyalty implied in Times correspondence; endorses “A Mahomedan”’s repudiation of the crime. Distinguishes a few misguided men from the community. Relationship of twelve–fourteen years with educated Bengal Muslims as former Principal of the Mohammadan College.
Letter II — Times (20 Oct. 1871)
Danger from Muslim malcontents can be reduced to a minimum. Muslims will live peaceably under British rule if considerately treated — even prefer it to likely native Muslim alternatives — but that is not enough: Britain claims moral superiority and must earn content. Discusses alleged discontent: Permanent Settlement’s effects; resumptions / Inám Commission; loss of revenue and judicial patronage as English education shifted posts to Hindus; vernacular press and educated aspirations. Government can still act.
Letter III — Times (2 Nov. 1871; signed Beachlands, Ryde, 30 Oct.)
First letter: loyalty; second: discontent; third: redress. Hard to undo Inám resumptions; easier to reform education and patronage. History of policy: Hastings founds Mohammadan College (own cost, then Directors’ land grant under Shore — Bengal’s “Haileybury”); Jones, Colebrooke, Macnaghten, Prinsep, Wilson, Gilchrist. Macaulay’s Anglicist victory: English as “key of knowledge”; Hindu College rises as Mohammadan College is sidelined; Muslims “ousted” from soil by Cornwallis and from patronage by 1835 education change. Halifax / 1854 Education Despatch: universities, English for higher, vernacular for lower; Oriental colleges maintained but not fitted into the scheme; no comprehensive India report to the Secretary of State despite Stanley and Northcote. Bengal University change wrecks Halifax’s link-scholarship fabric; talk of absorbing Mohammadan College into Presidency College. Proposal: Oriental Faculty beside English Faculty at Calcutta; affiliate Oriental colleges; classics as Latin/Greek; choice between thorough English with some Arabic/Sanskrit and thorough Oriental with some English. Pure English alone gives Muslims no influence with co-religionists. Frere on absence of public opinion.
Article — Influence of the late Prince Consort on university and popular education in England
Prince Albert and the elevation of national education; science in school and university; practical application of educating the whole social system, not only a favoured few. Bridge from English reform debates to Indian policy.
Four articles on education (Calcutta Englishman, 1866), including:
Of Lord Macaulay’s celebrated Education Minute — close reading and critique of the 2 Feb. 1835 Minute; Anglicist victory; what Auckland and the Directors later corrected; Latin/Greek analogy false (Sanskrit and Arabic hold that place in India); stipends and “useless” Oriental scholars; misreading of the 1813 Charter clause.
Of the impossibility of giving a National basis to a system of Public Instruction in which National Institutions and National Feelings are ignored — today’s question is not who won in 1835 but whether those principles remain sound; Cousin and Guizot as Western contrasts; Oriental vs English colleges as beacons of disunion.
Appendix — Lord Macaulay’s Minute (2 February 1835)
Full text of the Minute: construction of the 1813 lac; attack on Arabic and Sanskrit printing and stipends; English as key; Russian parallel; propose abolish Madrasa and Sanskrit College at Calcutta (keep Benares and Delhi without stipends); enlarge Hindu College and English schools; threaten resignation from the Committee if the old system stands.
Closing letter — Garcin de Tassy to the Times (Paris, 17 Nov.)
Clarifies Lees (vs Trevelyan): not a return to old policy; “Have as much English as you like, but do not forcibly exclude the Oriental classical languages.”
Notes

Contemporary-lens reading: post-Norman panic pamphlet that turns a loyalty scare into an education and patronage brief for Mayo’s India.
Distinct from W. W. Hunter’s 1871 Trübner tract with the rebel-conscience subtitle; that work is not this ZIP’s text.
Pairs with temple-india-in-1880 (Muslim temper, education) and the Ripon volumes (vernacular press, Ilbert years) for late-century Muslim–state questions.

sources/malcolm-life-of-clive-vol1.content:
Malcolm — Life of Robert, Lord Clive, Vol. I
Major-General Sir John Malcolm, G.C.B., F.R.S. (1769–1833) — The Life of Robert, Lord Clive: Collected from the Family Papers Communicated by the Earl of Powis. — In Three Volumes. Volume I. John Murray, Albemarle Street, London, 1836.
The first volume of Sir John Malcolm’s biography of Robert Clive (1725–1774), the soldier and statesman who established British East India Company rule in Bengal. Written by a fellow Indian army officer and diplomat who served in India during the same era (Malcolm was a key figure in the later Anglo-Maratha wars, and had access to the Powis family papers).
The volume contains 9,913 lines, extracted from a CreateSpace reprint (2016) of the 1836 original.
Copy of the source file, raw extract, and source page from the Great Britain 18th century wiki (great britain 18th century). Raw text also at raw/malcolm-life-of-clive-vol1/raw.txt.
Chapter Summary
INTRODUCTION — General View of the State of India in 1746. The decline of the Mughal Empire since Aurungzebe (1707), the rise of the Marathas, the European trading companies, the Portuguese decline, the English and French East India Companies, the Carnatic and its rulers, Dupleix and La Bourdonnais, the outbreak of the War of the Austrian Succession in India, the capture of Madras (1746), the siege of Pondicherry, the peace of 1748.
CHAPTER I — Clive’s family and boyhood. His early life in India. History of the Carnatic to 1750. Clive’s arrival at Madras as a writer (clerk) in the Company’s service, his depression and attempted suicide, his transfer to the military branch.
CHAPTER II — Wars in the Carnatic. The siege of Arcot (1751) and subsequent operations of Clive till 1752. Clive’s defence of Arcot with 200 men against 10,000, his sorties and eventual relief — the feat that made his reputation.
CHAPTER III — Clive returns to England (1753). Again sent to India in 1755. The capture of Gheriah. Operations in Bengal. Calcutta retaken from Suraj-ud-Daulah, and the peace forced upon the Nawab.
CHAPTER IV — The surrender of Chandernagore (the French settlement in Bengal). The quarrel with Suraj-ud-Daulah.
CHAPTER V — The intrigues at the court of Murshidabad. The conspiracy of Mir Jafar. The Battle of Plassey (June 1757) — Clive’s victory with 3,000 men against 50,000. Suraj-ud-Daulah deposed, Mir Jafar raised to the throne.
CHAPTER VI — Transactions subsequent to the Battle of Plassey. The settlement of Bengal, the imposition of the Company’s authority.
CHAPTER VII — State of parties in Bengal and at the court of Mir Jafar. Clive proceeds to Patna. He accepts the government of Bengal.
CHAPTER VIII — Clive’s expedition to occupy the Northern Circars. Intrigues at the court of Murshidabad. The Shahzada’s invasion of Bihar repelled by Clive. Clive receives a jaghir (land grant).

sources/malcolm-life-of-clive-vol2.title: Malcolm — Life of Robert, Lord Clive, Vol. II
sources/malcolm-life-of-clive-vol2.content:
Malcolm — Life of Robert, Lord Clive, Vol. II
Major-General Sir John Malcolm — The Life of Robert, Lord Clive. — Volume II. John Murray, London, 1836.
Copy of the source file, raw extract, and source page from the Great Britain 18th century wiki. Raw text also at raw/malcolm-life-of-clive-vol2/raw.txt.
Covers Clive’s later career from 1758 through his second administration of Bengal and his final return to England. The key events are the defence of Madras against Lally, the defeat of the Dutch in Bengal, Clive’s first return to England, his political battles at the India House, his return to Bengal as governor, and the acquisition of the Diwani (the revenue administration of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa) for the East India Company.
Chapter Summary
CHAPTER IX — The Northern Circars expedition under Colonel Forde (1758). The siege of Madras by the French Count de Lally. Clive’s correspondence and strategic direction from Bengal.
CHAPTER X — The Dutch armament against Bengal (1759), destroyed by Clive’s decisive action. Proceedings in England regarding the government of Bengal. Clive’s famous letter to Pitt the Elder proposing that the Crown take over the Indian possessions. Clive returns to England (1760).
CHAPTER XI — Clive in England. His private life and character — the Indian nabob in London, his wealth and estates, his peerage, his parliamentary career.
CHAPTER XII — Clive’s politics. His quarrel with Laurence Sulivan, the chairman of the East India Company. His right to the jaghir (land grant) disputed. The parties at the India House. The disasters in India during his absence. Clive called upon to resume the government of Bengal. He consents and sets out for India (1764).
CHAPTER XIII — State of India during Clive’s absence (1760–1765). Vansittart’s government. The deposition of Mir Jafar. The elevation of Mir Qasim. The massacre of Patna (1763) — the killing of 150 British prisoners by Mir Qasim. The restoration of Mir Jafar. The disorders in Bengal.
CHAPTER XIV — Clive assumes the government of Bengal (1765). The state of the country and the various services. Military arrangements. Negotiations with the Nawab of Bengal. Treaty with the Nawab-Vizier of Oudh. The settlement with the Emperor Shah Alam II. The Diwani acquired for the Company — the grant of revenue administration over Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa, making the East India Company the de facto ruler of 20 million people. Discontents in the civil service and Clive’s reforms.

sources/malcolm-life-of-clive-vol3.title: Malcolm — Life of Robert, Lord Clive, Vol. III
sources/malcolm-life-of-clive-vol3.content:
Malcolm — Life of Robert, Lord Clive, Vol. III
Major-General Sir John Malcolm — The Life of Robert, Lord Clive. — Volume III. John Murray, London, 1836.
Copy of the source file, raw extract, and source page from the Great Britain 18th century wiki. Raw text also at raw/malcolm-life-of-clive-vol3/raw.txt.
The final volume of Malcolm’s biography, covering Clive’s last years in India (1766–1767) and his final return to England, the parliamentary attacks on his reputation, and his death in 1774.
Chapter Summary
CHAPTER XV — The mutinous combination among the officers of the Bengal army (1766). Clive’s suppression of the “white mutiny” over the reduction of double batta — nearly 200 officers resigned their commissions. Clive’s display of resolve, the collapse of the mutiny, the punishment of the ringleaders.
CHAPTER XVI — Clive’s other reforms in Bengal. The salt monopoly controversy — Clive’s allocation of its profits to senior civil and military officers as a legitimate allowance. The administrative reforms, the regulation of trade, the suppression of private trading by Company servants.
CHAPTER XVII — Clive returns to England (July 1767). His shattered health, the waters at Bath. His welcome by the Court of Directors and the public. His correspondence with Orme the historian, providing materials for the continuation of the history of India. His retirement from active service.
CHAPTER XVIII — The parliamentary attacks on Clive (1772–1773). The inquiry into the East India Company’s affairs, the accusations of corruption against Clive. Clive’s great parliamentary defence — “I stand astonished at my own moderation.” His acquittal and vindication by the House of Commons. His declining health, his death by suicide (November 22, 1774). The assessment of his character and achievements.
