sources/mill-history-british-india-vol1.title: James Mill — The History of British India, Vol. I (Wilson 4th ed., 1840)
sources/mill-history-british-india-vol1.content:
The History of British India, Vol. I (Mill / Wilson, 1840)
James Mill; fourth edition with notes and continuation by Horace Hayman Wilson, Boden Professor of Sanskrit, Oxford. Volume I of eight (half-title: Mill’s History of British India, by Wilson. In Eight Volumes. Vol. I.). This volume: British intercourse to the Act of 6 Anne / Godolphin award (1711), then Mill’s long Hindu survey.
Completeness
Complete as Volume I of the 1840 Wilson edition. Not the complete History.

Half-title: eight volumes; this file VOL. I.
Closer: END OF VOL. I. (E. Varty, 27 Camomile Street, Bishopsgate); UCLA Southern Regional Library Facility copy, 600 OCR leaves.
Book I (Company to 1711) and Book II (Hindus: chronology, caste, government, laws, taxes, religion, manners) are present.
Wilson’s continuation and later Books live in vols II–VIII, not in this ZIP.

Mill first published 1817 (three volumes). This is the annotated 1840 Madden set.
Summary
Wilson’s editor’s preface: Mill claimed patient research and independent judgment; Wilson supplies omissions from documents Mill lacked (Malcolm, Clive and Munro biographies, Wellesley and Wellington despatches) and corrects inaccuracies from Mill’s never having been in India and slight knowledge of Eastern languages. Mill had argued those were qualifications; Wilson: they will convince few. Local knowledge is needed to weigh Indian evidence; Mill often trusts the weakest authorities. European-language stock is not enough for Hindu and Mohammedan history; Vedas, Puranas, native chronicles, better Ferishta still wanting when Mill wrote.
Mill’s own Book I: commencement of British intercourse until the Company on a durable basis by 6 Anne. Five chapters: efforts to begin trade until the change from a regulated to a joint-stock company; joint-stock 1612 to the third joint-stock 1631–2; third stock 1632 to coalition with the Merchant Adventurers 1657; that coalition to the project of a rival company; rival company to the Award of Godolphin, 1711.
Book II, Of the Hindus: chronology and ancient history; classification and distribution of the people; form of government; laws; taxes; religion; manners. Wilson notes in the extract (end of vol.) on native character in Calcutta, against a wholly dark picture.
Source
Mill, James. The History of British India. Fourth edition, with notes and continuation by Horace Hayman Wilson, M.A., F.R.S. Volume I. London: James Madden and Co., successors to Parbury & Co., 8 Leadenhall Street; L. A. Lewis, Fleet Street. MDCCCXL (1840). Printer: E. Varty, Camomile Street. OCLC 14982847. Local file: Anna’s Archive ZIP of Internet Archive ark+=13960=t9x06f174 (600 page OCR files).
Full raw text concatenated at raw.txt (1,245,484 bytes; 28,480 lines; sha256 e67ecc3f339d636fa75af62d7f2627581d97f09dcd688ecb9c5c5d3885460b23). OCR medium (broken words, long-s residue).
Contents
Printed contents: Preface; Glossary; Book I chs I–V (pp. 1–153); Book II chs I–VII (from p. 154; Manners from p. 437). Wilson’s notes are interleaved throughout (marked —W. against Mill’s —M.).
Preface of the Editor (Wilson)
Wilson grants Mill patient research and a school of independent judgment, then lists what the 1817 text could not use: unpublished papers, and later printed witnesses (Malcolm; lives of Clive and Munro; Wellesley and Wellington despatches). He rejects Mill’s claim that never having been in India, and slight knowledge of Eastern languages, were qualifications. Residence and dialects are needed to weigh Indian evidence; Mill, Wilson says, often trusts the weakest authorities or the least careful passages of the better ones. European-language stock is not enough for Hindu or Mohammedan history: Vedas, Purāṇas, native chronicles, and a trustworthy Ferishta were still wanting when Mill wrote.
Glossary
Listed in the contents at p. xxxvi of the printed volume (Indian and Company terms for the notes).
Book I — British intercourse to 6 Anne / Godolphin 1711
Chapter I — From the first efforts at an Indian trade to the change from a regulated to a joint-stock company
Mill opens with a full century of Portuguese monopoly after Vasco da Gama: exploration to Japan, island discoveries, conquests, and the flood of Eastern goods that had once been credited with raising Venice and delaying Constantinople’s fall. English attempts at a north-west passage (Frobisher’s ore that proved glittering sand; Davis’s straits) fail; a 1582 Cape voyage turns back from Brazil; a 1596 China voyage is wrecked. Drake’s circumnavigation and other successful runs then point the way. Adventurers form; Lancaster commands the first fleet; the charter of 31 December 1600 incorporates them as a body politic, in Mill’s view not remarkably unlike other trading charters of the age, yet the origin of a later anomalous power. Voyages remain separate adventures of subscribing groups under Company regulation until the Directors push a joint stock.
Chapter II — Joint-stock, 1612, to the third joint-stock, 1631–2
Until 1612 each voyage is the property of those who put money into that adventure. Directors argue that a joint stock concentrates management in the Governor and themselves; in 1612 they resolve that the trade shall be on a joint stock only. No fixed share-capital yet: members still subscribe unevenly, but into the Directors’ hands as one fund. £429,000 is raised and split into four successive yearly voyages. Mill follows the Company’s early eastern stations and contests from Bruce’s Annals, including the Dutch rivalry that later chapters resume.
Chapter III — Third joint-stock, 1632, to coalition with the Merchant Adventurers, 1657
A third subscription of £420,700 (1631–32) fits out seven ships; later seasons shrink to five then three, with cargoes unrecorded. Mill cannot tell whether earlier capital was repaid, though Directors are already without funds. Connexions on the Coromandel coast: Masulipatam factory restored and privileges from the King of Golconda; Mogul leave to trade at Piplee in Orissa; Bantam again a presidency over the eastern coast. Despair of beating the Dutch in the islands. Courten’s association, using Endymion Porter and the King’s favour after new arrangements with the Portuguese, appears as a licensed rival. The thread runs to the 1657 coalition with the Merchant Adventurers.
Chapter IV — Coalition with the Merchant Adventurers to the project of a rival company
After the Council of State decides for joint-stock trade, Company and Adventurers unite. A 1657–58 subscription reaches £786,000; whether the expected charter was actually received is left uncertain (Bruce found no copy). Adjustment with owners of the old funds; Dutch pressure on Portuguese Ceylon and a blockade of Goa, threatening Diu and Swally. The new stock is no more prosperous: feeble factories; two silent years of equipments; resolutions to drop out-stations and confine the peninsula to Surat, Fort St George, and their subordinates. Cromwell dies; Charles II; Polaroon delivered in “prepared desolation.” Petition for a new charter at the Restoration, granted with little organised opposition. The chapter closes as a new rival-company project comes into view.
Chapter V — Rival company to the Award of Godolphin, 1711
From the Restoration charter, Mill says, the monopoly is little disturbed except by crushable interlopers until 1682–83, when a subscription for a rival joint-stock is serious enough for King and Council. Bruce thinks the scare made the Company speak of equipments in “vague and hyperbolical” millions. Debts: opponents in 1676 put them at £600,000; Surat already £135,000 in 1674; Bengal agency authorised to borrow £200,000; dead stock at Bombay £300,000 — debts probably exceeding capital. Bantam lost in a local war (English accused the Dutch). The narrative then runs through the two companies’ parliamentary struggle to 6 Anne c. 17 and Godolphin’s award, 29 September 1708 (contents heading: 1711): London Company pays the United Company £96,615 4s. 9d. because Indian assets fall short of debts; English Company receives £66,005 4s. 2d. because its Indian effects exceed debts; a Bengal debt of Sir Edward Littleton remains on the English Company’s own account; British debts to be cleared by 1 March 1709, the London Company’s £399,795 9s. 1d. by three calls on proprietors. Mill ends Book I by announcing that English intercourse with India is now to become intimate and extensive — the subject of the next two books.
Book II — Of the Hindus
Chapter I — Chronology and ancient history of the Hindus
“Rude nations seem to derive a peculiar gratification from pretensions to a remote antiquity.” Mill classes Hindu claims with Irish, Tartar, English, Athenian, and Arcadian origin-legends, and with a Chaldee fragment of Babylonian ages. The chapter is a sceptical survey of Hindu chronology and ancient history as then available in European languages, with Wilson already interrupting on authorities.
Chapter II — Classification and distribution of the people
Transition from tribal independence to monarchy is slow: no common judge, no preconcerted punishment, then crowding, discord, and “superior spirits” who first found government on divine authority. Nowhere, Mill says, are laws more exclusively referred to the Divinity than in the “theocracy of Hindustan”: society, rights, even domestic custom by divine prescription. The four-varna scheme and the multiplication of castes follow. Wilson’s long note: caste among Buddhists is not original; multiplication of castes is the work of the people, not a code; the lowest native is a member of a class, unlike European paupers who are the true outcastes.
Chapter III — The form of government
After rank and occupation, the political establishment. “Among the Hindus, according to the Asiatic model, the government was monarchical, and, with the usual exception of religion and its ministers, absolute.” No idea of rule other than the will of a single person. Menu: a king formed of particles of the guardian deities; a child-king still a divinity in human shape; hatred of the king is death. Wilson had already flagged (at the laws chapter) that unbounded Brahman authority and unbounded royal power cannot both be simply true, and that in the original system the two were meant to check each other.
Chapter IV — The laws
Second determinant of political condition: how individual rights are expressed and secured. Materials are abundant; Mill offers only character and spirit, not an analysis of the whole code. Among rude peoples, maxims of justice are not kept distinct from other subjects; in Hindu law-books, jurisprudence occupies a moderate space beside religion, education, domestic custom, and private morality. Wilson vs Mill on English analogies (Hume, Blackstone, Paley, Bolingbroke on the Crown) and on the check between princes and Brahmans.
Chapter V — The taxes
Of government and law, nothing more decides happiness or misery than how the state’s pecuniary wants are met, and how far agents divide the annual produce of land and labour. Company servants’ financial perplexities of detail are set aside; Mill wants the outline in the ancient books. Menu: the king may take an eighth, sixth, or twelfth of grain (Culluca: by soil and labour); a sixth of the increase of trees, flesh, honey, ghee, perfumes, medicines, flowers, roots, fruit, leaves, pot-herbs, grass, leather, cane, earthen pots, stone-work; a fiftieth of the yearly addition to cattle, gems, gold, and silver. Other heads of levy follow in the ordinance list.
Chapter VI — Religion
Whether constitution and law or religion most sway Hindu lives is left open; priests, Mill says, obtained greater authority in India than anywhere, and multiplied the ideas on which their power stood. Laws, classification, and government are all “transacted by the Deity”; observances hedge every hour and function; meditation on divine attributes is the occupation that prepares the votary for participation in the divine nature. Only a general view is attempted: Brahman language on the gods is vague, fictions innumerable, ideas discrepant — “no coherent system of belief seems capable of being extracted.” Wilson’s notes on ritual and on Hindu “fate” as the consequence of past acts (not helpless destiny) sit against Mill’s picture.
Chapter VII — Manners
Manners = the peculiar modes of the ordinary business of life (eating, meeting, transacting, sport), which is everywhere the same business. So much of Hindu life is religious service that the religion chapter has already drawn the principal branch. Class distinctions: the lower orders “degraded below the brutes”; except Vaiśyas (agriculture and barter), productive classes are “vile and odious” by the standards of law and religion. Four āśramas for the honourable classes: student (more apprentice than literary pupil; even a Brahman’s child ranks as Śūdra before investiture), householder, forest penitent, sannyāsi. Wilson’s note D (end of the volume, after Calcutta residence): polished manners and independence among men of property; natives “estimable and amiable” who will requite kindness and justice from those who rule them.
Notes for later extraction
Needs remaining Wilson volumes. Pair Book I with bruce-annals-eic-vol1–bruce-annals-eic-vol3 and russell-short-history-eic. Entity/event pages await Proceed.

sources/mill-history-british-india-vol2.title: James Mill — The History of British India, Vol. II (Wilson 4th ed., 1840)
sources/mill-history-british-india-vol2.content:
The History of British India, Vol. II (Mill / Wilson, 1840)
James Mill; fourth edition with notes and continuation by Horace Hayman Wilson. Volume II of eight (half-title: Mill’s History of British India, by Wilson. In Eight Volumes. Vol. II.). Continues Book II of the Hindus from mill-history-british-india-vol1, then Book III on the Mohammedan conquerors through the Mughal dynasty.
Completeness
Complete as Volume II of the 1840 Wilson edition. Not the complete History.

Half-title VOL. II.; closer END OF VOL. II. (E. Varty, Camomile Street). 548 OCR leaves, Internet Archive ark+=13960=t5s758k6f.
Book II chs VIII–X and Book III chs I–V are present.
mill-history-british-india-vol3 now holds Book IV (1708–1773) and Book V chs I–II.

Summary
Mill finishes the Hindu survey with arts (architecture, weaving, jewellery; Chidambaram and Srirangam as European marvels he discounts), literature (almost all verse; history as narrative poems without resemblance to fact), and a long “General Reflections” on where Hindus sit on the scale of civilization — written, he says, because British government must be adapted to that scale, and because Britain has mistaken a people who have made “but a few of the earliest steps” for a highly civilized one. Wilson’s note at the head of those reflections: government should see Hindus as they are now, with a bias in their favour.
Book III: India at the Cape opening is a Muslim government and force over a Hindu population. Northern invasions (Scythians, Darius’s Indian satrapy, Alexander), then Ghaznavids to their expulsion; first Ghurid dynasty; second Ghurid/Afghan line to the Mughals; Mughal dynasty from the break-up of Timur’s empire and Baber, 1525, to its close; last a comparison of Muslim and Hindu civilization. Wilson’s closer on the comparison: Muslim literature never enlightened the people; governments military despotism; religion nearer truth than Hindu idolatry but as full of trifling observance and less humane in its intolerance than Hindu polytheism.
Source
Mill, James. The History of British India. Fourth edition, with notes and continuation by Horace Hayman Wilson. Volume II. London: James Madden and Co.; L. A. Lewis. MDCCCXL (1840). OCLC 14982847. Local file: Anna’s Archive ZIP hash 32d880599431da25f5009a3c269dfc9d.
Full raw text concatenated at raw.txt (1,099,449 bytes; 24,924 lines; sha256 86347bcf744588b6ef77d331c5b52babdcf9658cca464fa7a7eef66a6007d9eb). OCR medium.
Contents
Printed contents: Book II (continued) chs VIII–X (Arts; Literature p. 47; General Reflections p. 152); Book III The Mohammedans chs I–V (Ghaznavids p. 234; first Ghurid p. 259; second Ghurid/Afghan to Mughals p. 281; Mughal dynasty p. 319; comparison of civilization p. 479).
Book II (continued) — Of the Hindus
Chapter VIII — The Arts
Arts, necessary or ornamental, as a mark of progress. Hindus, Mill says, little courted the pleasures of the arts: houses of the great mean and almost unfurnished (Sir Thomas Roe: mud, one storey, except Surat stone; great men in tents for want of inheritance); food simple; dress distinguished only by fineness of texture. First arts of a rising people: hunting, shelter, covering; hence weaving and architecture early, then jewellery from the savage love of ornament. These three — architecture, weaving, jewellery — are the only arts for which the Hindus have been celebrated; except weaving they remained low. Robertson on the Chidambaram (Chillambrum) gopuram (122 feet, copper plates, 1332 × 936 feet) and Orme on Srirangam’s seven enclosures are treated as size plus “loose eulogy,” not proof of high civilization. Inferior as manufacturers to the Chinese; Jones’s slighting of Chinese arts is turned against his Hindu praise. Wilson: Hindu iron-smelting, welding, and steel are ancient (Ctesias); English iron-casting is recent.
Chapter IX — Literature
Literature as the surest inference to civilization, because it is the friend of useful knowledge. First literature is poetry (passions before speculation; verse as memory before writing). Hindu literature, Mill says, has always remained at this first stage: almost everything in verse; for history only narrative poems that “depart from all resemblance to truth and nature”; laws and sacred and scientific books in verse, as among other rude nations. Wilson: “permanent signs” cannot mean writing, which Hindus have had as long as a literature; metre continues because Sanskrit metre is easier, not because of German carmina antiqua.
Chapter X — General Reflections
To place Hindus on the scale of civilization is curiosity and, for Britain charged with their government, “the highest practical importance”: no scheme of government works unless fitted to the people’s state. If Britain has taken Hindus for a highly civilized people when they have made only the earliest steps, measures of government will miss the mark. The preceding induction — religion, laws, government, manners, arts, sciences, literature — is offered as the material for a correct judgment. Mill then attacks received claims of enormous riches found by the first Muslim conquerors (Ferishta followed by Dow as Eastern exaggeration that refutes itself); from his induction, poverty and wretchedness of the great body of the people in earlier as in European-witnessed times. Wilson’s head-note: British measures have little to do with Hindus in the days of Manu; see them as they are, with a bias in their favour; “We shall not promote their advance in civilization by treating them as little better than barbarians.”
Book III — The Mohammedans
Chapter I — First northern invasions to the expulsion of the Ghaznavid dynasty
When Europe opened the Cape route, the people of Book II had long been under a foreign race: Muslim government and force over a Hindu population, new forms in some departments of state, military command in foreign hands. Hindustan always subject to north-west incursions. Justin’s Scythians; Darius Hystaspes’ Indian satrapy (Herodotus: the most valuable of twenty; Rennell’s Indus/Punjab/Kabul/Kandahar — Wilson: Mill misquotes Rennell on Delhi). Alexander did not go as far as Darius. Then the Ghaznavid line in India to its expulsion, closing on Khosroo II, Mohammed of Ghur taking Ghazni/Kandahar, Multan, and advancing to Lahore.
Chapter II — First Ghurid dynasty to the second Ghurid or Afghan dynasty
After Khosroo’s defeat and death, Mohammed leaves India to a viceroy, returns to Ghazni, five years later marches on Ajmer, takes Tiberhind, is defeated and wounded near Thanesar by the rajas of Ajmer and Delhi, then returns with Turks, Persians, and Afghans. The combined rajas (Mill repeats the inflated 150 kings, 300,000 horse, 3,000 elephants) send an insulting offer of unmolested retreat; Mohammed feigns humility, crosses the river by night, and fights in four lines with a chosen horse reserve. The chapter is the first Ghurid hold in India until the second, Afghan, line.
Chapter III — Second Ghurid or Afghan dynasty to the commencement of the Mughal dynasty
Afghan/Delhi-sultanate narrative to the eve of Baber. The extract’s closer of this span: Ibrahim of Delhi twenty years against rebellion; in 1525 Baber, descendant of Timur, deprives him of throne and life.
Chapter IV — From the commencement to the close of the Mughal dynasty
Opens on the death of Shahrokh and the dissolution of Timur’s empire; Turks under the successors press Mesopotamia; Ismael the adventurer (1500). Then Baber’s line through the Mughal emperors to the dynasty’s close (printed contents from p. 319). This is Mill’s continuous political narrative of the Mughals, not a Company chapter.
Chapter V — Comparison of civilization: Muslim conquerors and Hindus
After the transactions of Book III, Mill asks the stage of civilization of the invading nations, and whether Hindu civilization rose or fell under Muslim ascendency. Western Asia (Persians, Arabians, even Turks) a degree higher than nations further east. The actual conquerors of Hindustan he places on a level with Arabians and Persians at their height: eastern Persian empire, Bactria and Transoxiana; language of Balkh as the elegant Persian, the tongue God uses mildly to the cherubim. Wilson’s end-note: Muslim literature original in part but less agreeable than Hindu except history; science borrowed from Greeks and Hindus; magnificence of the caliphs brief; letters confined to court and camp; governments military despotism; religion nearer truth than Hindu idolatry, in practice as full of trifling observance, and in intolerance less humane than Hindu polytheism.
Notes for later extraction

Pair Book III with bruce-annals-eic-vol1–bruce-annals-eic-vol3 for the Company side of the same centuries. Entity/event pages await Proceed.

sources/mill-history-british-india-vol3.title: James Mill — The History of British India, Vol. III (Wilson 4th ed., 1840)
sources/mill-history-british-india-vol3.content:
The History of British India, Vol. III (Mill / Wilson, 1840)
James Mill; fourth edition with notes and continuation by Horace Hayman Wilson. Volume III of eight (half-title: Mill’s History of British India, by Wilson. In Eight Volumes. Vol. III.). The Company’s political century: one exclusive corporation after Godolphin, to the first parliamentary reconstruction (13 Geo. III, 1773), then the opening of Hastings’s government under the new council.
Completeness
Complete as Volume III of the 1840 Wilson edition. Not the complete History.

Half-title VOL. III.; closer END OF VOL. III. (E. Varty). 672 OCR leaves, Internet Archive ark+=13960=t8sb40980.
Book IV chs I–IX (1708–1773) and Book V chs I–II (Hastings to Nuncomar, printed p. 515/584) are present.
Book V is advertised to Pitt’s Act 1784; the remainder is in Vol. IV.

Summary
After the union of 1708, Mill treats Company business as routine: proprietors and directors, an oligarchy in fact though a democracy on paper, ten India-House committees, export/import figures, chartered ships. Narrative then follows the Carnatic war and Mohammed Ali; Suraj-ud-Daulah, Calcutta, and Meer Jafar; Lally, Pondicherry, the French driven from the Carnatic; Meer Jafar’s first nabobship, Vansittart, Mir Qasim, inland-trade disorders, Oudh; Carnatic spoils after the French fall; Clive’s second coming, the Diwani, batta mutiny, dividend politics; Nizam Ali, the Northern Circars, first war with Hyder Ali; then English public opinion, supervisors, and the Act that changes the constitution. Book V opens with Hastings as Governor-General (revenue as Dewan, Rohillas, sale of Corah and Allahabad) and the new council’s split, Bombay and Ragoba, and Nuncomar hanged for forgery.
Source
Mill, James. The History of British India. Fourth edition, with notes and continuation by Horace Hayman Wilson. Volume III. London: James Madden and Co.; L. A. Lewis. MDCCCXL (1840). OCLC 14982847. Local file: Anna’s Archive ZIP hash 68bfbf3bb257c890f9a152ba9d25eab7. UCLA Southern Regional Library Facility copy.
Full raw text concatenated at raw.txt (1,259,395 bytes; 29,680 lines; sha256 b3034e928f6f91682ec1bec10f28d85dd13129c115863ca85f028c8be4b6fe8f). OCR medium.
Contents
Printed contents (incomplete in the scan after Book IV ch. III; remaining Book IV titles recovered from chapter headings): Book IV chs I–IX; Book V chs I–II.
Book IV — One exclusive Company, 1708, to 13 Geo. III, 1773
Chapter I — Constitution, India-House business, and transactions to Aix-la-Chapelle
Once competitors are one corporation with exclusive trade on statute, business becomes “regular and uniform”: fixed capital, recurring routine. Proprietors in General Court; twenty-four Directors (Chairman and Deputy), annually elected; vote on £500 stock, Director qualification £2,000; four regular courts a year. Supreme power theoretically in proprietors (legislation, dividend, annual displacement of Directors); in fact an oligarchy of Directors, because inspection is labour and the mass prefers to take for granted that all is well — the Bank of England and every joint-stock, Mill says, the same. Ten committees: Correspondence (prime governing business), Law-suits, Treasury, Warehouses, Accounts, Buying (lead and woollens), House, Shipping, Private Trade, and Preventing the Growth of Private Trade. Exports 1708 official £60,915 (bullion average next twenty years £442,350); imports 1708 £493,257, twenty-year average £758,042; sales by auction at the India House; Company prefers chartered ships. Narrative of the French war in the Carnatic down to Aix-la-Chapelle, including Labourdonnais and Dupleix (governor of Pondicherry from 1742; father a farmer-general and EIC director). Wilson on Orme vs Labourdonnais’ Mémoire over the naval feint.
Chapter II — Contest for establishing Mohammed Ali, Nabob of the Carnatic
Origin, progress, and suspension of the war that puts Mohammed Ali on the Carnatic masnad: Dupleix’s revolutions, English and French as king-makers, Arcot and the Carnatic succession (printed from p. 85).
Chapter III — Suraj-ud-Daulah, Calcutta, Meer Jafar
Bengal and Orissa under Aurangzeb’s grandson Azim-ush-Shan; deputy Jafar Khan; Aliverdi; the youth Suraj-ud-Daulah succeeds, “more than the usual share of the princely vices.” First act: plunder of his aunt. Takes Calcutta; army from Madras; dethroned; Meer Jafar set up (Plassey implied in the heading’s “in his stead”). Seir Mutaqherin, Orme, Holwell, Scrafton weighed in the notes.
Chapter IV — Renewal of the French war in the Carnatic; Lally; Pondicherry taken
When the Calcutta detachment and Bussy’s relief leave the Carnatic, both sides wait: English for Bengal troops, French for a European armament. Mohammed Ali is without a rival, yet the Carnatic’s produce is small; governors, zamindars, polygars withhold; his rabble cannot collect. Lally arrives; French power superior, then English; Pondicherry taken; French driven out of the Carnatic.
Chapter V — First nabobship of Meer Jafar; Vansittart; Mir Qasim; Jafar restored; Clive sent back
“A defective treasury is the grand and perennial source of the difficulties which beset the sovereigns of India,” pressing peculiarly on Meer Jafar after Plassey: Aliverdi’s Maratha war, Suraj’s profligacy, sums promised to purchase the English conspiracy, chiefs impatient, troops in arrear. Expedition against the Northern Circars; Emperor’s eldest son with the nabobs of Oudh and Allahabad invade Bengal; Clive resigns, Vansittart succeeds; Jafar dethroned, Meer Casim set up; disorders of the servants’ private trade; war with Casim; Jafar restored; war with Oudh; Jafar dies, his son a nominal nabob; Proprietors and Directors; Clive sent back to govern Bengal.
Chapter VI — Political state of the Carnatic after the French fall
By the final overthrow of the French, the British have more than they hoped: not only a grateful nabob but one dependent, “the whole kingdom of the Carnatic subject to their absolute will.” The difficulty is the split of powers between nominal and real sovereign; few things regulated by agreement; each party inwardly resolved to appropriate. Views of the nabob on Vellore, Tanjore, the Marawars; treaty with Tanjore; Company’s jaghir; war on Mohammed Issoof; mound of the Cauvery.
Chapter VII — Clive’s second administration; the Diwani
Clive, Sumner, and Sykes arrive Calcutta 3 May 1765 to form the Select Committee (Carnac with the army, Verelst at Chittagong). They assume extraordinary powers though the original “disturbances” are over. Company’s orders on private trade disregarded; arrangements with the Vizir and the Emperor; acquisition of the Diwani; private trade made a monopoly for superior servants; reduction of military allowances (batta) and its effects (officers’ combination); Clive resigns, Verelst succeeds; dividend proceedings in England; financial difficulties; Verelst resigns, Cartier succeeds.
Chapter VIII — Northern Circars, Nizam Ali, Hyder Ali
Carnatic again pressed by neighbours. Nizam Ali imprisons his brother (18 July 1761) and takes the Deccan. Treaty of Paris (10 Feb. 1763) as proof that good Indian government cannot be made by rulers sitting in Europe. English take the Northern Circars; treaty with the Subahdar embroils them with Hyder Ali; Hyder’s history; first war with the English; new treaty with the Subahdar; peace with Hyder. Wilson sends the reader to Wilks’s Historical Sketches of the South of India.
Chapter IX — Public opinion, Parliament, and the change of constitution (1773)
Conflicting passions in England; expired dividend restriction of 1767; Directors petition against renewal as subverting charter. Plan of Supervisors; plan of a King’s Commissioner; pecuniary difficulties; dividend raised; Company unable to meet obligations; parliamentary inquiry; ministerial relief; an Act which changes the constitution of the Company (13 Geo. III); tendency of the change; financial and commercial state. Clive’s Commons speech vindicating his conduct appears in the debates Mill follows.
Book V — From the 1773 change to Pitt’s Act, 1784 (this volume: two chapters)
Chapter I — Hastings until the parliamentary councillors arrive
Hastings appointed Governor-General; Clavering, Monson, Barwell, Francis the Council, not removable except by the King on the Directors’ representation. Hastings’s rise: council in Vansittart’s time; Madras 1769; Bengal government succeeding Cartier, 1772. Arrangements for collecting revenue and administering justice ostensibly as Dewan; treatment of Mohammed Reza Khan and Raja Shitabroy; elevation of Munny Begum; destruction of the Rohillas; sale of Corah and Allahabad to the Vizir; payment of the Emperor’s revenue refused; financial results.
Chapter II — New government; Ragoba; Nuncomar
New constitution to commence in India after 1 August 1774; Clavering, Monson, and Francis arrive 19 October; old government dissolved. Council splits; Governor-General in the minority. Bombay espouses Ragoba, ejected Peshwa; Supreme Council condemns and makes peace with his opponents (Salsette among the cessions). Upper-country powers: Oudh, Emperor, Najaf Khan. Alleged pecuniary corruption (Rani of Burdwan, faujdar of Hugli, Munny Begum); Hastings resists inquiry; Nuncomar the accuser, prosecuted, convicted of forgery, hanged; Mohammed Reza Khan and the naib-subah office restored. Volume ends on the majority’s scheme of upholding a “country government” pretext for dealing with foreign factories.
Notes for later extraction
Continues mill-history-british-india-vol1–mill-history-british-india-vol2. Pair Book IV with malcolm-life-of-clive-vol1–malcolm-life-of-clive-vol3 and russell-short-history-eic. Remaining Book V (to 1784) and Wilson’s later volumes are still to come. Entity/event pages await Proceed.

sources/mill-history-british-india-vol4.title: James Mill — The History of British India, Vol. IV (Wilson 4th ed., 1840)
sources/mill-history-british-india-vol4.content:
The History of British India, Vol. IV (Mill / Wilson, 1840)
James Mill; fourth edition with notes and continuation by Horace Hayman Wilson. Volume IV of eight (half-title: Mill’s History of British India, by Wilson. In Eight Volumes. Vol. IV.). Hastings’s second half: after Nuncomar, the Governor-General recovers a majority, fights Marathas and Mysore, squeezes Benares and Oudh, and is reconstructed from Westminster by Pitt’s Act.
Completeness
Complete as Volume IV of the 1840 Wilson edition. Not the complete History.

Half-title VOL. IV.; closer END OF VOL. IV. (E. Varty, 27 Camomile Street). 606 OCR leaves, Internet Archive ark+=13960=t1ng4jh52.
Book V chs III–IX (printed pp. 1–582) are present. This volume completes Book V (the 1773 change to Pitt’s Act 1784), which opened in Vol. III with chs I–II.
Wilson’s continuation (later volumes) is not in this file. Book VI opens in Vol. V.

Summary
The quinquennial farm of 1772 is running out; Monson dies; Hastings recovers the governing vote. Annual settlements, a disowned resignation, Middleton/Fowke/Munny Begum, Directors disobeyed; Leslie/Goddard across India; Bombay’s Poona failure; Francis duels Hastings and goes home. Madras: Nabob, royal plenipotentiary, Tanjore twice, Pigot imprisoned, Rumbold and Guntoor. French war, Pondicherry, Hyder overruns the Carnatic, Baillie cut off, Coote, Macartney, Hyder dies, Tippoo, Matthews, Mangalore, Fullarton, peace. Goddard, Sindia, the Supreme Court’s reach, Impey at the Sudder Dewannee, a new Board of Revenue. Hastings to Benares: Chet Singh arrested, country taken, Directors condemn. Oudh: Begums despoiled, eunuchs tortured, ten lacs, Fyzoolla Khan; Hastings resigns. At home: charter, Select and Secret Committees, Dundas, Fox’s two bills, Pitt’s East India Bill.
Source
Mill, James. The History of British India. Fourth edition, with notes and continuation by Horace Hayman Wilson. Volume IV. London: James Madden and Co.; L. A. Lewis. MDCCCXL (1840). OCLC 14982847. Local file: Anna’s Archive ZIP hash 9c2a4a0b5557fb96f90f944e2c54e8ac. UCLA Southern Regional Library Facility copy.
Full raw text concatenated at raw.txt (1,128,450 bytes; 26,959 lines; sha256 9f8c3ce19d383c9e1814b2fd6fcc59c64b980a5803b370180fdf3b49505ede68). OCR medium.
Contents
Printed contents: Book V chs III–IX.
Book V continued — From the 1773 change to Pitt’s Act, 1784 (this volume: chs III–IX)
Chapter III — Revenue after 1772; Hastings recovers power; Marathas; Francis’s duel
The five-year farm of 1772 is drawing to a close. The 1773 experiment had already abolished collectors, grouped the provinces into six divisions (Calcutta, Burdwan, Moorshedabad, Dinagepore, Dacca, Patna) under chiefs and councils, with native naibs/aumils in Dewannee Adaulut. Colonel Monson dies; Hastings recovers the governing majority. He plans an inquiry into the sources of revenue; taxes levied by annual settlements. A resignation is tendered in London by an agent whom Hastings disowns. Middleton, Fowke, Munny Begum: Directors order reversals; Calcutta disobeys. Maratha relations; a Bengal detachment sent across India to Surat; Bombay’s expedition against Poona fails; fruitless negotiation; Goddard’s campaign; connexion with the Ranna of Gohud. Francis fights a duel with Hastings and returns to Europe. Directors (Mill quotes) had preferred Ragoba and Bassein to Upton’s Poona treaty; Leslie is to march via Berar; Poonah factions (Siccaram Baboo, Nana Furnavese, Sindia) turn the Bombay policy on and off.
Chapter IV — Carnatic, Tanjore, Pigot, Rumbold
On the Coromandel coast the Company’s relation to the country is different from Bengal. English and Nabob; a royal plenipotentiary with independent powers; Hyder Ali and the Marathas court and threaten both. Nabob and plenipotentiary want a Maratha alliance; the Presidency holds to neutrality. Relations with the King of Tanjore: hesitation, then war, war on the Marawars, a second war on Tanjore, condemned by the Directors. Pigot sent out to restore the Raja; opposition in the Madras Council; Pigot imprisoned. Committee of Circuit; Governor Rumbold suspends it and summons the zamindars to Madras. Transactions with Nizam Ali respecting Guntoor, censured by the Supreme Council; Rumbold and others condemned and punished by the Court of Directors.
Chapter V — French war, Hyder, Coote, Macartney, Tippoo
War with the French is no longer the first Indian danger; still Pondicherry is taken. War with Hyder Ali; the Presidency unprepared; Colonel Baillie’s detachment cut off. The Supreme Council suspends the Governor of Fort St. George and sends Sir Eyre Coote to Madras. Hyder takes Arcot and overruns the greater part of the country. Lord Macartney Governor of Fort St. George. Negapatnam and Trincomalee taken from the Dutch. Treaty with the Nabob of Arcot; assignment of the Nabob’s revenues. Tellicherry invested; great armaments from England and France; Brathwaite’s disaster in Tanjore; Madras reduced to famine. Death of Hyder Ali; Tippoo withdraws the Mysorean army from the Carnatic. Operations and fate of General Matthews on the Malabar coast; siege of Mangalore; the General at Madras, refusing to obey civil authority, arrested and sent to Europe. French and English suspend hostilities on news of European peace. Colonel Fullarton in Coimbatore; peace with Tippoo; behaviour of the Supreme Council to Madras.
Chapter VI — Goddard, Sindia, Supreme Court, Board of Revenue
Return to Bengal while the south burns. Finances distressed in every Presidency; Bombay cannot pay the army. Goddard on the Bombay side of the Maratha country; attack on the Bengal side; peace with Sindia. The Supreme Court of Judicature tries to extend its jurisdiction: effects on individuals, on revenue collection, on the administration of justice. Parliament is asked to interfere, and does: the Chief Justice placed at the head of the Sudder Dewannee Adaulut, then recalled. Judicial and police regulations; provincial councils abolished; a new Board of Revenue set up.
Chapter VII — Benares; Chet Singh; Maratha peace
Immediately after those financial and judicial changes, Hastings journeys to the Upper Provinces. History of the Company’s connexions with the Raja of Benares; requisitions; resolution to relieve the Company’s necessities by forcible exaction. Hastings arrives; the Raja put under arrest; a tumultuous assemblage; affray with the soldiers; the Raja escapes; war, country subdued. Directors condemn Hastings. Double negotiation with the Marathas of Poona; treaty of peace. (Mill’s notes send the reader to the Sixth Report of the Select Committee 1782 and the impeachment papers.)
Chapter VIII — Oudh, the Begums, resignation
The Nabob of Oude is deeply in arrear; his country disordered. Complaints; how the English receive them. Bristow removed; agreement between Hastings and the Nabob; the Begums despoiled; whether they excited insurrection; alleged oppressions of Colonel Hannay; the head eunuchs tortured; a present of ten lacs to Hastings. Hastings accuses Middleton and replaces Bristow. Treatment of Fyzoolla Khan. Directors’ decision on the Begums set at nought. New accusations against Bristow; plan to remove the residency; Hastings repeats his visit to Oudh; resigns the government. Financial results of his administration; incidents at Madras.
Chapter IX — Charter, committees, Dundas, Fox, Pitt
From the last great legislative interference: 1767–1773 the Company paid the public £400,000 a year “in respect of the territorial acquisitions”; in 1773 embarrassment forced a loan of £1,400,000. Legislative proceedings 1773–1780; renewal of the charter; Select and Secret Committees of the House of Commons; proceedings against Indian delinquency. Mr. Dundas’s East India Bill; Mr. Fox’s East India Bills; Mr. Pitt’s East India Bill. Mill’s closer: Pitt’s machinery at home, control of Bengal over the other Presidencies, aggressive wars and presents forbidden, displaced zamindars to be restored, Arcot debts and Tanjore disputes referred to the Directors. Wilson’s note defends Hastings against “pitiful dissection of his private” acts.
Notes

Continues mill-history-british-india-vol3 (Book V chs I–II, Nuncomar). Completes Book V.
Same 1840 Madden/Wilson set as vols I–III. Wilson’s continuation (post-Mill narrative) belongs in later volumes.
Printer: E. Varty (OCR also “VAKTT”).
Contemporary-lens reading: this is the volume that feeds the later Hastings impeachment (Benares, Begums, presents) and the Board of Control settlement of 1784.

sources/mill-history-british-india-vol5.title: James Mill — The History of British India, Vol. V (Wilson 4th ed., 1840)
sources/mill-history-british-india-vol5.content:
The History of British India, Vol. V (Mill / Wilson, 1840)
James Mill; fourth edition with notes and continuation by Horace Hayman Wilson. Volume V of eight (half-title: Mill’s History of British India, by Wilson. In Eight Volumes. Vol. V.). After Pitt’s Act: Macpherson, Dundas’s Board of Control, Cornwallis, the Hastings trial in Westminster Hall, the war with Tippoo, and the Permanent Settlement.
Completeness
Complete as Volume V of the 1840 Wilson edition. Not the complete History.

Half-title VOL. V.; closer END OF VOL. V. (E. Varty). 664 OCR leaves, Internet Archive ark+=13960=t06w98086.
Book VI chs I–VI are present. Book VI is advertised from the 1784 constitution to the termination of the war with the Mahrattas in 1805; the remainder is in Vol. VI.
Continues mill-history-british-india-vol4 (end of Book V / Pitt’s Act).

Summary
Hastings leaves; Macpherson (ex-purser, Arcot confidential) takes the chair. Dundas’s Board of Control pays the Nabob of Arcot’s debts without inquiry, gives up the Carnatic assignment, and absorbs the Directors. Cornwallis is appointed. Commons begin the Hastings impeachment (articles of charge; Impey’s motion fails; Pitt’s declaratory act). Chapter II is the trial, opening Westminster Hall 13 February 1788. Cornwallis: Oudh troops and money, Guntoor from the Nizam, Travancore lines, alliance with Nizam and Marathas, Medows in Coimbatore, Tippoo down the Gujelhutty Pass. Cornwallis takes command: Bangalore, Seringapatam, Arikera, distress of bullocks, third campaign, camp stormed, peace with Tippoo. Then the great internal revolution: financial and judicial reforms (zamindars, collectors, courts) and, in ch. VI, Mill’s verdict that the project of a landed aristocracy failed, with a closer on Indian surplus as parliamentary song over a coming deficit (from 1797).
Source
Mill, James. The History of British India. Fourth edition, with notes and continuation by Horace Hayman Wilson. Volume V. London: James Madden and Co.; L. A. Lewis. MDCCCXL (1840). OCLC 14982847. Local file: Anna’s Archive ZIP hash 0a4488182a615176e31fdf768d4823d5. UCLA Southern Regional Library Facility copy.
Full raw text concatenated at raw.txt (1,250,066 bytes; 29,626 lines; sha256 ae61db3084426c6e8c4e6ea4d6e3a62cc000623b483bf1a534acf73aeb29aff9). OCR medium.
Contents
Printed contents: Book VI chs I–VI.
Book VI — 1784 constitution to the Maratha war of 1805 (this volume: six chapters)
Chapter I — Macpherson; Board of Control; Cornwallis; Hastings impeachment begun
Hastings gone, Macpherson as senior in council is Chief Governor (1785). Mill’s sketch: sailed to Madras 1766 as purser; insinuated into the Nabob of Arcot’s confidence; sent to the Duke of Grafton to plead the Nabob’s “oppressions”; later a factor writing Dupre’s despatches; unsigned memorial under Pigot; dismissed. Internal and external state of the Indian government. Board of Control (Dundas) pays Arcot debts without the inquiry Pitt’s Act seemed to give the Directors (three classes: 1767 loan, cavalry loan, 1777 consolidated debt; twelve lacs a year appropriated). Orders the Carnatic revenue assignment given up; absorbs the power of the Directors. Lord Cornwallis appointed Governor-General. Parliamentary proceedings toward Hastings’s impeachment: best mode rejected; articles of charge; three bills to amend the East India Act; impeachment voted; Impey motion negatived; Pitt’s declaratory act. Wilson on Sindia, Gholam Kadir, Shah Alam blinded, Juwan Bukht.
Chapter II — The trial of Mr. Hastings
Westminster Hall, 13 February 1788. Queen and princesses in the Duke of Newcastle’s gallery; Mrs Fitzherbert in the royal box; Prince of Wales and royal dukes; two hundred Commons; managers in full dress (Fox among them). Mill follows the spectacle and the course of the trial as a set piece of English public life about Indian government.
Chapter III — Oudh, Guntoor, Travancore, first Mysore campaign
Cornwallis takes the reins September 1786 with a joint Board/Directors code. Arrangement about troops and money with the Nabob of Oude. Guntoor Circar obtained from the Nizam; new arrangement whose aspect toward Tippoo Saib is hostile. Tippoo’s dispute with the Raja of Travancore; attack on the Travancore lines; English prepare for war; alliance with Nizam and Marathas. Plan of campaign: General Medows takes Coimbatore and a chain of depots to the bottom of the Gujelhutty Pass; Tippoo descends the pass and forces the English back to the Carnatic. End of campaign; Cornwallis arrives at Madras; Malabar operations; new arrangement with Mohammed Ali on Carnatic revenues.
Chapter IV — Cornwallis in command; Bangalore to peace with Tippoo
Cornwallis meant to take the war himself, deferred when Medows got Fort St. George, resumes when the first campaign falls short. Siege of Bangalore; march to Seringapatam; Bombay army; battle at Arikera; army in distress for bullocks and provisions, obliged to return. Maratha contingent; negotiations; Commons debate on the war. Third campaign: fortresses commanding Carnatic passes reduced; Nizam’s army and Maratha contingent between the two marches on Seringapatam; Bombay army; Tippoo’s operations; march; entrenched camp stormed before Seringapatam; preparations for siege; negotiations; peace; subsequent (and judicial) arrangements.
Chapter V — Cornwallis’s financial and judicial reforms
Internal government “not less memorable” than foreign transactions. Revenue first in the new India code: predecessors censured (farmers and temporary agents instead of permanent zamindars; collectors excluded from assessments; heavy arrears; country exhausted). The reforms that follow are the Permanent Settlement and the Cornwallis judicial system (Mill’s authorities: the 1793 Code of Regulations and the Fifth Report of 1810).
Chapter VI — Result of those reforms
Mill jumps chronology to survey institutions and results together. Immediate object: a landed aristocracy in the persons of the zamindars. “That project … has completely failed.” Default of tax; sale of estates; the closer is fiscal: ministers sang surplus (India a “vast source of wealth”) while from 1797 a permanent deficit began, charge of new conquests swelling to its limits.
Notes

Book VI continues in Vol. VI (to 1805 Maratha war).
Same 1840 Madden/Wilson set as vols I–IV.
Printer: E. Varty (OCR also “VARTT”).
Contemporary-lens reading: Board of Control vs Directors on Arcot paper; Hastings as Westminster theatre; Cornwallis as both soldier against Tippoo and author of the zamindar settlement Mill says failed.

sources/mill-history-british-india-vol6.title: James Mill — The History of British India, Vol. VI (Wilson 4th ed., 1840)
sources/mill-history-british-india-vol6.content:
The History of British India, Vol. VI (Mill / Wilson, 1840)
James Mill; fourth edition with notes and continuation by Horace Hayman Wilson. Volume VI of eight (half-title: Mill’s History of British India, by Wilson. In Eight Volumes. Vol. VI.). Wellesley’s decade: 1793 charter, Shore, fourth Mysore war, subsidiary system, Maratha war, Holkar, and Mill’s own close at 1805.
Completeness
Complete as Volume VI of the 1840 Wilson edition. Not the complete History.

Half-title VOL. VI.; closer END OF VOL. VI. (E. Varty). 708 OCR leaves, Internet Archive ark+=13960=t08w39s69.
Book VI chs VII–XIII are present. This volume completes Book VI (1784 constitution to the Maratha war of 1805), which opened in Vol. V with chs I–VI.
Mill stops here: “official papers … are not sufficiently at command. Here, therefore, it is necessary that, for the present, this History should close.” Wilson’s continuation opens in Vol. VII.

Summary
Parliament renews the Company’s charter in 1793 (Dundas’s surplus theatre, 3,000 tons of private shipping, Board salaries). Shore succeeds Cornwallis: Nizam and Marathas, death of Mahadaji Sindia, Peshwa, Tippoo’s hostages restored, Oudh succession (Wazir Ali dethroned as “spurious,” Saadat Ali set up), death of Mohammed Ali, Hobart vs the Supreme Board, Dutch settlements taken. Mornington (Wellesley): Tippoo’s agents at the Isle of France, immediate war, Nizam’s French dismissed, Seringapatam taken, Sultan killed, country divided. Oudh: military “reform” as annihilation, half the country ceded, Henry Wellesley on the commission, Farrukhabad assumed. Surat, Tanjore, Arcot nabobs/raja deposed. Subsidiary system pressed on the Peshwa; Treaty of Bassein; Sindia and Berar; Lake in the north (Aligarh, Delhi, Laswari), Wellesley in the south (Assye, Argaum, Gawilgarh); treaties. Holkar: Monson’s retreat, Delhi defended, Deeg, Farrukhabad, Bhurtpore fails; Cornwallis returns to unwind Wellesley’s alliances; dies; Barlow adheres; treaties with Sindia and Holkar; financial results. Mill then closes the series of British transactions.
Source
Mill, James. The History of British India. Fourth edition, with notes and continuation by Horace Hayman Wilson. Volume VI. London: James Madden and Co.; L. A. Lewis. MDCCCXL (1840). OCLC 14982847. Local file: Anna’s Archive ZIP hash d3559efe4e23a53e27d726e86639e84c. UCLA Southern Regional Library Facility copy.
Full raw text concatenated at raw.txt (1,316,891 bytes; 31,320 lines; sha256 e039a77faf2d68ed9bc92423be45e4548aac810179910decc80b042ab3bc8250). OCR medium.
Contents
Printed contents: Book VI chs VII–XIII.
Book VI continued — 1784 to the Maratha war of 1805 (this volume: chs VII–XIII)
Chapter VII — 1793 charter; Shore; Oudh succession; Hobart; Dutch settlements
Exclusive privileges near expiry; Liverpool, Glasgow, Paisley, Manchester, Norwich, Exeter petition for a free Eastern trade. Ministers keep Pitt’s system. Dundas displays a favourable balance (Wilson/Tucker: 1792–3 surplus about £1.86m including Tippoo money, then decline to deficit 1797–8). Proposed appropriation of a supposed £1,239,241 surplus: £500,000 to Indian debt, £500,000 tribute to the nation, dividend 8 to 10 per cent; Company still needs the equivalent of a £2m loan (capital increased at 200). Board of Control gets salaries; 3,000 tons private shipping (no military stores, no piece goods; Company’s warehouses and sales). Dundas vs “theory”: union of government and commerce, monopoly. Sir John Shore succeeds Cornwallis. Relations with Nizam and Marathas; death of Mahadaji Sindia; war Nizam–Marathas; Peshwa dies; Tippoo fulfils treaty, hostages restored. Nabob of Oude dies; son dethroned as spurious; Saadat Ali made nabob. Madras: Mohammed Ali dies; Lord Hobart wants transfer of part of the nabob’s country; dispute with the Supreme Board. Dutch settlements captured.
Chapter VIII — Mornington; fourth Mysore war; Seringapatam; Tippoo killed
Lord Mornington Governor-General. Tippoo’s agents at the Isle of France; Mornington resolves on immediate war. Nizam Ali takes more English troops and dismisses the French; fruitless negotiations at Poona; demands escalate. Campaign; siege of Seringapatam; army short of food; Seringapatam taken, the Sultan killed; division and settlement of the conquered country.
Chapter IX — Oudh: subsidiary army, cession, Henry Wellesley
Oudh as left by Teignmouth (Shore) satisfied the home authorities. Mornington meditates great changes: extirpation of British subjects not in Company service; Afghan scare; Sindia alliance dropped; embassy to Persia; Vizir Ali’s insurrection. Military “reform” pressed on the nabob = annihilation of his army; he offers to abdicate for his son, refuses to abdicate for the Company; coercion. Want of resources for the British army used to infer the need to take his government; more than half the country taken by force; no independent power in the rest. Hon. H. Wellesley sent to get an appearance of consent; commission for the ceded districts; Farrukhabad assumed. Directors object to H. Wellesley’s appointment; Board of Control overrules. Home authorities fully approve the settlement.
Chapter X — Surat, Tanjore, Arcot deposed
City of Surat, once the greatest maritime commerce of India (Tapti, Persian and Arabian gulfs, hajj port). Nabob of Surat deposed; Raja of Tanjore deposed; Nabob of Arcot deposed. (Heading in the extract also notes the Governor-General resigns — Wellesley’s later departure sits with the close of the volume.)
Chapter XI — Subsidiary system; Treaty of Bassein; path to Maratha war
Two sets of princes: those made to resign both military and civil power, those made to resign only the military. Attempt 1798–1802 to make the Peshwa resign the military part; similar negotiation with Daulat Rao Sindia fails. War Sindia–Holkar; Peshwa driven from Poona; for restoration by English arms he consents; Treaty of Bassein. Mornington expects other Maratha states will not dare quarrel; Sindia marches to Burhanpur; Peshwa restored; Sindia and the Raja of Berar join; English require them to quit a menacing position; they evade; treated as enemies. Mill investigates Mornington’s arguments that the line of policy was good.
Chapter XII — Lake and Wellesley; Aligarh, Delhi, Assye; treaties
Northern objects / southern objects / minor objects. Lake takes the field: French force in Sindia’s service and his Doab possessions; Shah Alam continued; battle of Aligarh and capture of the fort; battle of Delhi, emperor surrenders to the English; Agra; Laswari; French force destroyed, Doab transferred. General Wellesley in the south: Ahmednagar; Assye; Burhanpur and Asirgarh; Sindia’s overture; Argaum; siege of Gawilgarh. Operations in Bundelkhand, Cuttack, Gujarat. Treaties with Berar and Sindia; engagements with minor princes near the Jumna; Sindia enters the defensive alliance. Mill investigates the Governor-General’s account of the benefit of defensive alliances and the Maratha war.
Chapter XIII — Holkar, Monson, Bhurtpore, Cornwallis/Barlow; Mill closes
Necessity of curbing Holkar; Mornington would take his dominions and give them to Peshwa, Sindia, and Nizam. Holkar retreats; Commander-in-Chief cantons, leaving Colonel Monson in advance; Holkar turns; Monson’s disastrous retreat to Agra. Gujarat army subdues Holkar in Malwa; stratagem on Delhi, brave defence; Deccan dominions subdued; infantry beaten at Deeg, cavalry routed at Farrukhabad. Raja of Bhurtpore joins Holkar; unsuccessful attack on the fortress; accommodation. Disputes with Sindia; Holkar joins Sindia’s camp; resident ordered out. Marquis Wellesley succeeded by Marquis Cornwallis: unwind subsidiary/defensive alliances, yield to Sindia, restore Holkar’s territories, dissolve connexions with minor frontier princes. Cornwallis dies; Sir G. Barlow adheres. Holkar among the Sikhs; Lake pursues; fresh treaty with Sindia; treaty with Holkar; financial results. Mill: subsequent events not sufficiently at command; the History closes. Wilson’s note on Company trade accounts.
Notes

Completes Book VI and Mill’s own narrative (to 1805). Wilson’s continuation is vols VII–VIII of this set.
Same 1840 Madden/Wilson edition as vols I–V.
Printer: E. Varty (OCR “VARTV” / “VAHTY”).
Contemporary-lens reading: Dundas’s 1793 surplus as parliamentary persuasion; subsidiary alliance as a machine for taking armies then territory; Mill writing as a critic of Wellesley from the India House generation.

sources/mill-history-british-india-vol7.title: H. H. Wilson — The History of British India, Vol. VII (continuation, 1845)
sources/mill-history-british-india-vol7.content:
The History of British India, Vol. VII (Wilson continuation, 1845)
Horace Hayman Wilson, continuing James Mill. Volume VII of eight (half-title: Mill’s History of British India, by Wilson. In Eight Volumes. Vol. VII.). Title-page of this volume: The History of British India, from 1805 to 1835, London, Madden, 1845. Wilson’s own Book I (printed signatures still say VOL. I) covers 1805–1813.
Completeness
Complete as Volume VII of the Madden set. Not the complete History. (Vol. VIII’s half-title revises the set to nine volumes.)

Half-title VOL. VII.; 640 OCR leaves, Internet Archive ark+=13960=t8bg2kk3s. Printer S. & J. Bentley, Wilson, and Fley (no “END OF VOL.” line; closes on the 1813 resolutions / appendix).
Wilson’s Book I chs I–VIII plus appendix (1813 parliamentary resolutions). Advertised span 1805–1835; this volume stops at the 1813 charter. Remainder begins in Vol. VIII.
Continues mill-history-british-india-vol6, where Mill closed at 1805.

Summary
Wilson’s advertisement (25 Nov. 1844): he promised to carry Mill to the last charter renewal; India House records (Hobhouse, Bayley), parliamentary prints, and contemporary narratives took longer than expected. Book I then surveys the post-1805 political map (Delhi, Oudh, Nizam, Peshwa, Gaekwar, Berar, Sindia, Holkar, Amir Khan, Rajputs, Bhurtpore, Sikhs and Ranjit Singh). Barlow: retrenchment, Cuttack/Doab/Bundelkhand, Vellore mutiny (religious panic at military orders), Bentinck and Cradock recalled. England: Lauderdale blocked, Barlow recalled by sign-manual, Minto appointed; Paull’s impeachment of Wellesley abandoned. Minto: Bundelkhand, Sutlej Sikhs, embassy to Peshawar/Shah Shuja, Sindh, Malcolm vs Harford Jones in Persia. Madras: Travancore insurrection, officers’ mutiny (tent contract, Munro, Macdowall, Seringapatam garrison), Barlow finally recalled. Foreign: Amir Khan, Joasmi pirates, Macao, Bourbon, Isle of France, Moluccas, Java (Minto present, Raffles governor). Internal: Oudh, civil-court arrears, dakoiti, zamindari vs ryotwar, Serampore missionaries, Fort William College. Close: Company loan, 1813 charter — India trade opened, China reserved, 13th resolution on useful knowledge and missionaries.
Source
Wilson, Horace Hayman. The History of British India, from 1805 to 1835. Issued as Volume VII of Mill’s History, fourth edition with notes and continuation. London: James Madden and Co. M.DCCC.XLV (1845). OCLC 14982847. Local file: Anna’s Archive ZIP hash bc328bf7452edfb3e576188634863214 (copied from Downloads into the India folder). UCLA Southern Branch copy.
Full raw text concatenated at raw.txt (1,220,747 bytes; 27,994 lines; sha256 89aa4990bcd365145ddab5bd13d82a60a2199b09d30bde7377cff1001dcc36fd). OCR medium.
Contents
Printed contents: Wilson Book I chs I–VIII; appendix.
Book I (Wilson) — Peace with the Marathas, 1805, to charter renewal, 1813
Chapter I — Political map after 1805
Hostilities with the principal Maratha chiefs have altered relative position; Barlow’s government, impatient of financial pressure, “threw away some actual and some prospective advantages.” Native princes: King of Delhi (Prince Jehangir); Nawab of Oude; Nizam (Mahipat Ram, Mir Alam); Peshwa; Gaekwar and Kathiawar; Raja of Berar (Sambalpur relinquished); Sindia and Bhopal; Holkar (Kandi Rao, Kasi Rao, Tulasi Bai regent); Amir Khan. Rajputs: Udaipur, Jodhpur, Jaipur — contest for Krishna Kumari; British refuse Jaipur; princess dies. Bikaner, Kota, Bundi, Macheri; Jats, Bhurtpore; Gohud treaty annulled. Sikhs: origin, constitution, rise of Ranjit Singh.
Chapter II — Barlow; Vellore
Finances, retrenchments; judicial/revenue for Cuttack, Doab, Bundelkhand; settlements in ceded and conquered provinces; Madras separates judicial and revenue. Murder of Europeans at Vellore; dragoons; fort retaken. Origin: religious panic from military orders; similar alarms at Hyderabad, Walajabad, Nandidrug. Lord W. Bentinck and Sir John Cradock recalled.
Chapter III — England: Minto; Wellesley impeachment
Directors refuse Lauderdale; Barlow recalled by the King’s sign-manual; Lord Minto appointed. Mr Paull’s impeachment of Wellesley (Oudh, Farrukhabad, Sasni); dissolution; Folkestone; impeachment abandoned; condemnatory resolutions negatived. Carnatic inquiry motion fails. Proprietors censure Wellesley. Select Committee; diminished Company import trade.
Chapter IV — Minto: Bundelkhand, Sikhs, Afghanistan, Sindh, Persia
Order in Bundelkhand: Ajaygarh, Gopal Singh, Kalinjar, Rewa, Hariana. Sikh chiefs east of the Sutlej taken under protection; treaty with Ranjit Singh. Embassy to Peshawar; Shah Shuja; mission to Sindh fails. France and Persia: Sir Harford Jones from England vs Sir John Malcolm from India; Jones reaches Tehran, preliminary treaty disavowed then confirmed; Sir Gore Ouseley definitive treaty “productive of little advantage.”
Chapter V — Madras: Travancore; officers’ mutiny
Barlow unacceptable at Madras. Sherson; Carnatic debt commission; Reddy Rao. Travancore: Dewan vs Resident; Cochin; Resident’s house attacked; St. Leger; Arambuli lines; Dewan dies, brother executed, body gibbeted; Resident as Dewan. Commander-in-chief refused a Council seat. Tent contract; officers demand court-martial on Colonel Munro; Macdowall arrests him, government cancels, Macdowall sails; Boles suspended; Hyderabad, Masulipatam, threatened march on Madras; test to European officers; Seringapatam garrison in open rebellion; Close at Hyderabad; Minto arrives; courts-martial; Auchmuty C-in-C. Directors restore officers; Barlow finally recalled.
Chapter VI — Foreign policy: pirates, islands, Java
Amir Khan in Berar; Peshwa and southern jagirdars; piracy of Wari and Kolhapur; Joasmis, Ras-al-Khaima. Macao. French cruisers; Rodriguez; Bourbon; Grand Port disaster then Isle of France (Port Louis). Moluccas: Amboyna, Banda, Ternate. Java: Minto accompanies; Batavia, Weltevreden, Fort Cornelis (Gillespie), Janssens surrenders; Raffles governor; Yogyakarta; Palembang sultan deposed. Wilson: beneficial results of British administration in Java; Directors’ views.
Chapter VII — Internal: Oudh, courts, dakoiti, revenue, Serampore
Minto back from Java. Hyderabad and Nagpur; Oudh misgovernment; Resident vs Nawab. Civil courts multiply suits and arrears; criminal arrears; police; dakoiti; native co-operation excluded then half-recovered; superintendents of police. Revenue review: sovereign proprietary right Mohammedan not Hindu; village communities; zamindar; Madras ordered a permanent zamindari settlement, then ryotwar, then village settlements; Directors prohibit perpetual settlement at Madras and in the ceded/conquered provinces of Bengal. House-tax at Benares repealed; religious riot; Serampore missionaries checked; Fort William College; close of Minto’s administration.
Chapter VIII — 1813 charter
Embarrassed finances; parliamentary loan; patronage abuse. Dundas vs the Court; ministers determine to open the trade with India; Company accedes; China reserved. Outports; Buckinghamshire; Castlereagh resolutions. Hastings and others on unrestricted Europeans and missionaries. Commons and Lords; Proprietors accept. Appendix prints the resolutions, including resolution 13: promote useful knowledge and religious and moral improvement, with facilities for persons going to India, local governments’ authority preserved, natives’ free exercise of religion “inviolably maintained.”
Notes

This is Wilson’s continuation, not Mill’s text. Title-page date 1845 (Mill vols I–VI of this set were 1840).
Wilson Book I = set Vol. VII. Printed running heads still say BOOK I / VOL. I.
A second Mill ZIP (503b8996…) was still downloading in Downloads at extract time (empty/incomplete); not used.
Contemporary-lens reading: Barlow as financial unwind of Wellesley; Vellore as sepoys reading dress orders as religion; 1813 as the India trade opened and the missionary clause written as a Commons resolution.

sources/mill-history-british-india-vol8.title: H. H. Wilson — The History of British India, Vol. VIII (continuation, 1846)
sources/mill-history-british-india-vol8.content:
The History of British India, Vol. VIII (Wilson continuation, 1846)
Horace Hayman Wilson, continuing James Mill. Volume VIII (half-title: Mill’s History of British India, by Wilson. In Nine Volumes. Vol. VIII.). Title-page: The History of British India from 1805 to 1835, Volume II, Madden and Malcolm, 1846. Wilson’s Book II covers the Earl of Moira / Marquis of Hastings, 1813–1823.
Completeness
Complete as Volume VIII. The set is no longer eight volumes.

Vol. VII’s half-title said eight volumes; this volume’s half-title says nine. Wilson Volume II = set Vol. VIII. 644 OCR leaves, Internet Archive ark+=13960=t3nv9c64q. Bentley printer; no “END OF VOL.” line; closes on finance appendix tables (revenues 1813–14 to 1822–23).
Wilson Book II chs I–XII (1813 charter to close of Hastings, 1823). Advertised span 1805–1835; remainder is Vol. IX.
Continues mill-history-british-india-vol7 (Wilson Book I to 1813).

Summary
Earl of Moira (October 1813) finds the treasury exhausted and war overdue. Nepal / Gorkha war: Kalanga (Gillespie killed), Ochterlony at Malaun, Kumaon, Makwanpur, peace and cessions west of the Jumna. Ceylon: Kandy taken, lost, king deposed; rebellion. Cutch, Baroda, Hyderabad princes, Oudh loans, Bareilly house-tax, Hatras, Cuttack rising. Poona: Gangadhar Shastri murdered, Trimbak; Nagpur subsidiary alliance; Holkar/Tulasi Bai; Amir Khan in Rajputana. Pindaris (Cheetoo, Karim) force an offensive; Trimbak escapes; new treaty with the Peshwa. Campaign 1817–18: Kirki, residency burned, Peshwa flees; Sitabaldi and Nagpur; Mahidpur and Holkar treaty; Pindaris hunted; Koregaon; Satara raja proclaimed, Peshwa deposed. Talner, Malegaon, Gonds/Bhils, Apa Saheb in the Mahadeo hills. Central India settlement; Cutch, Sindh. Internal: courts told to revert toward native institutions; magistrate-collector; ryotwar vs village settlement; Malwa opium, salt; Bishop Middleton and Bishop’s College; Scottish church; missionary schools; censorship of the press abolished. Close of Hastings; revenue up from £17.2m (1813–14) to £23.1m (1822–23).
Source
Wilson, Horace Hayman. The History of British India, from 1805 to 1835. Volume II. London: Madden and Malcolm, 8 Leadenhall Street. M.DCCC.XLVI (1846). Issued as Volume VIII of the Mill/Wilson set. OCLC 14982847. Local file: Anna’s Archive ZIP hash 503b8996ca0d2e35592f6e2fb6483a91. UCLA Southern Branch copy.
Full raw text concatenated at raw.txt (1,185,455 bytes; 27,836 lines; sha256 6d9ac265390fdddce240aedcfd4445014480c9d3430d1935557829bb98152f20). OCR medium.
Contents
Printed contents: Wilson Book II chs I–XII; appendix of revenue tables.
Book II (Wilson) — 1813 charter to the close of the Marquis of Hastings, 1823
Chapter I — Moira; Nepal war opened (Kalanga, Ochterlony, Malaun)
Moira appointed after Perceval’s death (cabinet negotiation for the Prince Regent); combined Governor-General and Commander-in-Chief; Calcutta October 1813. Treasury barely covers current spend; Canton bills; establishments cut too low. Nepal 700 miles of frontier; Gorkhas under Prithi Narayan; Bhotwal/Gorakhpur, Saran, Bettia. War proclaimed. Second division: three failures at Kalanga, Gillespie killed, fort evacuated. Martindell at Nahan/Jytak. First division: Ochterlony turns Ramgarh, invests Malaun.
Chapter II — Nepal war finished; Kumaon; treaty
Third division (Wood) fails at Jitpur. Fourth: Tirai, Marley’s alarm, Gorkhas abandon the Tirai; Sikkim alliance. Kumaon: Gardner, Hearsay taken, Nicolls, Almora; Kumaon and Garhwal ceded. Jytak blockaded; Deothal; Bhakti Thapa killed; Amar Singh capitulates; country west of the Jumna ceded. Delays; hostilities renewed; Ochterlony, Churia-ghati, Makwanpur; peace. Wilson considers objections to the war; votes of thanks; results.
Chapter III — Ceylon, Cutch, Hyderabad, Oudh, Bareilly, Cuttack
Kandy: embassy, war, capital taken, Mutu-sami, Davie, Europeans murdered; king captured and sent to Madras; Ceylon subject; rebellion and pretender suppressed. Cutch anarchy; Anjar; pirate states; Baroda. Nizam’s sons to Golconda. Sadat Ali dies; Ghazi-ud-din; loans; Resident removed. Bareilly house-tax tumult; Dayaram of Hatras. Cuttack: assessments, land sales, Puri taken and recovered; special commission.
Chapter IV — Poona, Nagpur, Holkar, Rajputana
Peshwa and Trimbak Rao; Gangadhar Shastri’s mission to Poona; murder at Pandharpur; Trimbak given up, confined at Thane. Nagpur refuses then, after the raja’s death, Apa Saheb as regent accepts subsidiary alliance; Bhopal siege. Holkar: adopted son, Tulasi Bai, Balaram Seth killed, Tantia Jog. Rajputana wasted by Amir Khan; Man Singh feigns imbecility.
Chapter V — Pindaris; policy of total suppression; Trimbak’s rising
Pindaris on the Narmada: Sindia-shahi and Holkar-shahi; Cheetoo, Karim, Dost Mohammed; raids on Nizam, Peshwa, Berar, then British districts (Mirzapur, Masulipatam, Guntur, Circars). Moira for total suppression; Board of Control limits Jaipur alliance then modifies; council opposition. Alliances with Rajputs, Amir Khan, Bhopal. Trimbak escapes; insurrection; Poona surrounded; new treaty, extra subsidiary force, territorial cessions; Gaekwar arrangements.
Chapter VI — Campaign of 1817–18; Kirki; Pindaris hunted
Grand army in Hindustan and army of the Deccan. Peshwa’s ultimatum; residency destroyed; battle of Kirki; Peshwa defeated and flees; Vaughans murdered; Poona occupied. Pindaris driven; Hislop near Ujjain; treaty with Sindia; cholera in the centre division; Amir Khan disbands; Cheetoo toward Jawad.
Chapter VII — Sitabaldi; Mahidpur; Peshwa deposed
Apa Saheb; Sitabaldi; Doveton; Jabalpur; Nagpur stormed, Arabs; Tulasi Bai murdered; battle of Mahidpur; Malcolm; Holkar treaty. Pindari leaders hunted (Karim, Cheetoo); lands in Bhopal and Gorakhpur. Smith after the Peshwa; Koregaon (Staunton); Satara taken, raja proclaimed, Peshwa formally deposed.
Chapter VIII — Talner, Khandesh, Malegaon
Armies dissolved; Hislop south; Talner stormed, kiladar hanged; hill forts; Arab mercenaries; siege of Malegaon; Narmada valley.
Chapter IX — Gonds, Bhils, Apa Saheb in the Mahadeo hills
Hill races; Bhils in Khandesh and Malwa; Apa Saheb’s refuge; Sparkes killed; Gond villages destroyed; insurrection checked.
Chapter X — Settlement of Central India
Holkar’s territories improve; Dhar and Dewas; Sindia’s contingent; Bhopal (Islamnagar restored).
Chapter XI — Cutch, Sindh, and miscellaneous after the war
Rao of Cutch deposed, infant and regency, subsidiary treaty. Amirs of Sindh; Khosa robbers; treaty. Other arrangements (Kota and neighbouring states in the heading).
Chapter XII — Internal administration; press; close of Hastings
Civil judicature inefficient; home authorities tell India to revert toward native institutions. Magistrate and collector united; village police. Land revenue: ryotwar to be general, perpetual settlement prohibited; village settlement in the west; special commission on fraudulent transfers; Madras village settlements closed, ryotwar resumed; Bombay/Broach/Gujarat surveys; Deccan mix. Opium (Malwa), salt, customs; British goods duties remitted. Finance: local surplus, home charges unmet, debt up; territorial vs commercial accounts. Calcutta an episcopal see (Bishop Middleton, Bishop’s College); Scottish church; missionaries and schools; censorship of the press abolished. Close of the administration. Appendix: revenue £17.228m (1813–14) to £23.120m (1822–23).
Notes

Wilson’s continuation, not Mill. Date 1846. Running heads BOOK II / VOL. II.
The Madden set is nine volumes from this half-title on. Vol. IX (1823–1835) is not in the folder.
Contemporary-lens reading: Nepal as a frontier war the previous governments deferred; Pindari suppression as the lever that finishes the Peshwa; Hastings as legislator (press, bishops, surveys) as well as soldier.

sources/mill-history-british-india-vol9.title: H. H. Wilson — The History of British India, Vol. IX (continuation, 1848)
sources/mill-history-british-india-vol9.content:
The History of British India, Vol. IX (Wilson continuation, 1848)
Horace Hayman Wilson. Volume IX of the Madden set (half-title: Mill’s History of British India, by Wilson. In Nine Volumes. Vol. IX.). Title-page: The History of British India from 1805 to 1835, Volume III, James Madden, M.DCCC.XLVIII (1848). Wilson’s Book III: close of Hastings, 1823, to close of Bentinck, 1835.
Completeness
Complete as Volume IX of nine. Completes Wilson’s advertised continuation (1805–1835).

Half-title IN NINE VOLUMES. VOL. IX. Wilson’s own title VOLUME III. Google Books PDF, 709 leaves (hash a125295ee516e46cfd00f58af45bc8db); image scan, Tesseract extract.
Book III chs I–IX. Closer of the narrative is the 1833 charter and “termination of Company’s commercial existence,” then a general index to the whole Mill/Wilson History.
Continues mill-history-british-india-vol8 (Hastings to 1823). Mill’s own text ended at mill-history-british-india-vol6.

Summary
Canning is named Governor-General, then Castlereagh dies and he stays in the Commons; Amherst (late China envoy who would not kowtow) takes India. John Adam in the interval: press, Hyderabad/Palmer & Co., debt interest 6 to 5 per cent. Amherst walks into war with Ava: Arakan fugitives, Shahpuri, Kachar; Rangoon taken and starved in the rains; Ramoo disaster; Barrackpore mutiny; Bandoola killed at Donabew; Treaty of Yandabo. Then 1825 unrest and Bhurtpore stormed; Ochterlony dies; Amherst to Simla, Ranjit Singh, Munro dies, Amherst goes home. Bentinck: half-batta, Malwa opium passes, rent-free tenures, native judges, suttee abolished, Bombay Supreme Court habeas fight, thugs, English education, steam. Disturbances: Khasia, Kachar, Naning, Kol, Mysore raja deposed, Coorg annexed, first Council of India. Native states under “non-interference” that Wilson calls partial and mischievous; Fraser murdered; Oudh; Ranjit and Shah Shuja. England: Select Committees, China monopoly, 1833 Act — Company ceases to trade.
Source
Wilson, Horace Hayman. The History of British India, from 1805 to 1835. Volume III. London: James Madden, 8 Leadenhall Street. M.DCCC.XLVIII (1848). Issued as Volume IX of the Mill/Wilson set. Local file: Anna’s Archive PDF hash a125295ee516e46cfd00f58af45bc8db (Google Books scan).
