Contents
Printed contents: Book III chs I–IX; then a set index.
Book III — Close of Hastings, 1823, to close of Bentinck, 1835
Chapter I — Adam, Amherst, origins of the Burma war, Rangoon
Directors name Canning (Board of Control 1816–20). Castlereagh dies; Canning stays to lead the Commons. Amherst appointed: credit from the 1816 China embassy, refusal of humiliation at Peking. Hastings leaves January 1823; John Adam until Amherst in August: press; Hyderabad and Palmer & Co. (advance to pay the Nizam, house interdicted); debt interest cut. Eastern frontier almost unknown: Assam, Garos, Kasiyas, Jyntia, Kachar, Manipur, Arakan under Ava. Burma took Arakan 1784; fugitives in Chittagong; Shore and Wellesley; Symes missions; Khyen-bran. Shahpuri island; Kachar fights; proclamation of war; expeditions from Bengal and Madras; Rangoon taken; population deserts; rains; Shwe-dagon occupied.
Chapter II — Assam, Ramoo, the lines at Rangoon
Operations in Assam and Kachar; detachment at Ramoo; Burmas cross in force; irregulars misbehave; sipahis fly; alarm at Chittagong and Calcutta; Burmas inactive, panic subsides. Negrais and Cheduba reduced. Rangoon lines harassed; stockades stormed; Kemendine evacuated and held; sickness.
Chapter III — Barrackpore; Arakan
Mutiny at Barrackpore: troops collected, mutineers fired on, some executed, rest pardoned. Arakan: estuaries of the Naf and Myoo, Koladyne, Kiung-pala, hills turned, town occupied, enemy leaves the province; Sandoway and Ramri; no pass to Ava; extreme sickness, town abandoned.
Chapter IV — Donabew to Yandabo
Pegu invited to elect a prince; cooperation not received. Campbell advances, land and water; Bassein; Donabew; land column to Tharawadi and Yuadit, back to Donabew; water column too weak until junction; elephants’ sally; death of Bandoola; Donabew evacuated; Prome for the rains; Siamese on Tenaserim; armistice, Kyi Wungyi; terms refused; Watigaon reverse; Burma army defeated; Melloon carried; Pagahm; final defeat; Treaty of Yandabo; return; Wilson on whether the war was inevitable and what it was worth.
Chapter V — 1825 unrest; Bhurtpore; close of Amherst
Feeling in Hindustan: protected Sikhs, Kunjawa, Hariana, Kalpee, Malwa rumours, Bhils, Coolies, Kittur, Kolapur, Cutch, Sindh. Alwar; assassination attempt on Ahmed Baksh Khan. Bhurtpore: infant raja, guardian murdered, Durjan Sal; Ochterlony assembles a force, government countermands, Ochterlony resigns and dies; then a large force, mines, storm, Durjan Sal taken. Alwar submits. Amherst up-country: Oudh loans, death of the king; Holkar; death of Daulat Rao Sindia, Baizi Bai; Delhi; Simla; Ranjit Singh; Syed Ahmed; Persia–Russia, subsidy ends, Abbas Mirza dies. Judicial talk; death of Sir Thomas Munro; finances; bishops; education; La Pérouse search. Amherst goes home.
Chapter VI — Bentinck: half-batta, opium, suttee, courts, thugs, English
W. B. Bayley until Bentinck. Economical reform; half-batta retrenchment, memorials, Directors maintain it; finance committees. Malwa opium: treaties with princes fail, opium passes succeed. Rent-free tenures, special commissioners. Commissioners of revenue and circuit; native judges. Suttee: officers consulted, arguments both ways, Governor-General prohibits, regulation, no resistance, Madras and Bombay, Hindu petition, counter-petition, Privy Council dismisses the appeal. Converts’ hereditary rights. Madras/Bombay enactments; separate legislation dropped. Bombay Supreme Court: Moro Raghunath, habeas corpus, Grant’s petition, court closed and reopened; Privy Council against the court’s pretensions; legislative member of Council. Hills; NW Provinces settlement. Thugs hunted. Education: exclusive English proposed and objected to. Steam to Europe; commerce; finance.
Chapter VII — Disturbances; Naning; Mysore; Coorg; first Council of India
Mohammedan fanatics near Calcutta. Eastern frontier: Singphos; Kasya Hills, Bedingfield and Burlton murdered; Tirath Sing imprisoned; Kachar raja assassinated, country annexed; Jyntia land sequestrated; Tenaserim (Tavoy, Mergui); Naning (Malacca), Panghulu, Madras reinforcements, annexed. Western frontier: Sambhalpur, Kol rising in Chota-Nagpur, Bamanghati, Burrabhim, SW frontier commissioner; Northern Circars. Mysore: raja’s misgovernment, insurrections, raja deposed, commissioner. Governor-General at Madras. Coorg: raja’s cruelty, four-division invasion, surrender, annexed. Nilgiris. First Council of India; change of system proclaimed; return to Bengal.
Chapter VIII — Native states; non-interference; Indus; Ranjit; Shah Shuja
Protective policy abandoned; non-interference “partial and mischievous”; extra-Indian interference authorised. King of Delhi’s agent in England; interview declined; Fraser assassinated. Oude: minister guaranteed then dismissed, Hakim Mehdi’s reforms, threatened deposal, intrigues. Nizam dies; successor wants British officers out; Palmer & Co.; Directors vs Board, mandamus. Bhopal; Ghaffar Khan and Amir Khan at Ajmer. New Indus policy from England; commercial treaties; interview with Ranjit Singh; Shah Shuja fails to recover Kabul. Marathas: Nagpur given back; Apa Saheb in Jodhpur; Gaekwar; Holkar dies, Hari Holkar; Gwalior soldiery, Baizi Bai to the Deccan. Rajputs: Kota partition, Bundi, Udaipur, Jodhpur (Man Sing, Dhokal Sing), Jaypur (Jota Ram, Blake murdered). Sirohi; Bikaner, Jaisalmer, Bahawalpur.
Chapter IX — 1833 charter; Company ceases to trade
Charter ending; Select Committees of both Houses; four times appointed, sub-committees. China monopoly. Court vs ministers: “paper of hints”; India still to the Company; territorial charges paid from trade; Grant: property to territory, dividends on territory; guarantee fund; Proprietors’ ballot. Claims: Oude bankers, Nozid zamindar, Hutchinson. Grant in Parliament; Wynn, Buckingham; Ellenborough and Wellington oppose. Directors object to a fourth presidency, abolition of subordinate councils, extra councillor, more bishops, change in civilian appointments. Petitions not received. Commons passes the bill; Proprietors accept on ballot; law; termination of the Company’s commercial existence; concluding remarks.
Notes

Completes the Madden nine-volume set and Wilson’s 1805–1835 continuation. Vol. VII said eight volumes; Vol. VIII revised the count to nine.
Google scan includes a general index to the whole History after the narrative.
Contemporary-lens reading: Burma as Nepal-plus-marsh; Barrackpore as sepoys refusing a stockade war; Bentinck as half-batta plus suttee plus English; 1833 as the Company stripped of the China trade.

sources/modern-india-and-the-west.title: L. S. S. O’Malley, ed. — Modern India and the West (1941)
sources/modern-india-and-the-west.content:
Modern India and the West (O’Malley, ed., 1941)
A Royal Institute of International Affairs symposium, edited by L. S. S. O’Malley with a foreword by Lord Meston, in which British and Indian specialists describe the nature, extent, and effects of Western civilization on Indian life and thought from Vasco da Gama’s landfall at Calicut (1498) through Company and Crown rule, and the far smaller reverse influence of India on the West.
Summary
The book’s object, stated in the preface, is a synopsis of Western influence on India since the beginning of the sixteenth century, of class and period reactions, and of India’s influence on the West. Work was directed by a special committee of Chatham House; opinions remain those of the individual writers. O’Malley frames the survey against Sir Richard Temple’s India in 1880 and Lord Ripon’s 1882 observation that education, a free press, legal for discretionary administration, railways and telegraphs, and easier communication with Europe were already producing marked change. The twentieth century, the preface says, has brought levelling ideas of a modern democratic nation; some see India taken in tow by the West, others the constants that persist (plus ça change).
Lord Meston’s foreword refuses the metaphor of a “clash”: the fitting image is a stream of new thought flowing into the sea of India’s traditions. Education is named the chief channel; English as medium at secondary and university stages is the long controversy. One side of the shield is deflection of vernacular intellectual genius; the other is new conceptions of speech, criticism of authority, and rights. Meston puts the test as whether Western teaching has given India the will and power to use unfamiliar political institutions for civic sense, national unity, and the greater happiness of the people. O’Malley died while the book was in the press; Meston records that he had given his best through much ill health.
Design: one author with special knowledge for each prominent phase of civilized life. Disappointments and omissions are admitted (literature confined to six leading vernaculars). O’Malley himself wrote the two opening chapters, Mechanism and Transport, the Hindu Social System, and the long General Survey; Meston calls the opening pair and the close a masterly aperçu of the whole Indian situation. Sir Benjamin Lindsay died during the progress of the work; his Law chapter remains.
The printed contents run: Foreword (Meston); Preface; I Historical Background (O’Malley); II Impact of European Civilization (O’Malley); III Law (Lindsay); IV Education (Cunningham); V The Press (Wordsworth); VI Mechanism and Transport (O’Malley); VII Economic Development (Anstey); VIII The Christian Ethic and India (Mayhew); IX Hinduism and the West (Radhakrishnan); X The Hindu Social System (O’Malley); XI Muslim Culture and Religious Thought (Yusuf Ali); XII Primitive Tribes (Hutton); XIII The Progress of Women (Gray); XIV Literature and Drama (Bengali, Hindi, Marathi, Tamil, Telugu, Urdu); XV Indian Influence on the West (Rawlinson); XVI General Survey (O’Malley); Index (printed p. 813).
Source
O’Malley, L. S. S. (Lewis Sydney Steward), 1874–1941, ed. Modern India and the West: A Study of the Interaction of Their Civilizations. With a foreword by The Lord Meston. London, New York, Toronto: Oxford University Press, 1941. Published under the auspices of the Royal Institute of International Affairs. First published 1941; reprinted lithographically in Great Britain at the University Press, Oxford, by Vivian Ridler, 1968. Local file: Internet Archive / Anna’s Archive PDF (OCLC 1150836198); 856 PDF pages.
Full raw text extracted from the local PDF via pdftotext -layout at raw.txt (2,494,984 bytes; 39,429 lines; sha256 4e832c7ca3a5ad563823811035fb35cea6fcc7b0ed8038c1712a746db040a6a2). OCR/layout: form-feeds, broken hyphenation, and scattered character substitutions (e.g. “IIP” for III in a running header). Chapter boundaries recovered from CHAPTER headings and the printed contents.
Contents
Foreword (Lord Meston) and Preface
Meston: impact of restless sceptical West on static contemplative East; India chosen because of special knowledge and because she may soon decide how far the impact is to carry her. Slow peaceful penetration rather than clash. Law largely accepted while family law preserved; literature imitates (Toru Dutt, Mrs. Naidu); music remains an exception. Nation-building services, especially education, met with zealous approval. Jowett quoted: Englishmen cannot govern a people without understanding it through languages, literature, institutions, customs, poetry and mythology, land and agriculture. Preface: cooperative survey under Chatham House; Temple 1880 and Ripon 1882 as benchmarks of already-visible change; tension between rapid Western advance and the unchanging East.
Chapter I — The Historical Background (L. S. S. O’Malley)
“The statement that India is not one country, but many countries, containing not one people but many peoples, has been repeated so often that it has become somewhat trite.” O’Malley accepts diversity and rejects the corollary of no unity: India is united by a common culture of remarkable continuity. What Isocrates said of Greece might be said of India: the name of a culture, not of a race. Self-insulated Hindu civilization with limited foreign traces (Mauryan–Persian contact, Greek medicine and astronomy, Gandhara). India as a geographical and cultural continuum. The chapter sets the pre-European civilizational frame against which later impact is measured.
Chapter II — The Impact of European Civilization (L. S. S. O’Malley)
“A new epoch in the history of India may be said to have begun in 1498, when Vasco da Gama’s three little ships cast anchor off Calicut.” First Portuguese objects: “Christians and spices” — crusade and the spice trade. Subsequent European nations follow. The chapter narrates the long impact from sea-route contact through commercial companies to territorial sovereignty, as the frame for the specialist chapters that follow.
Chapter III — Law (Sir Benjamin Lindsay)
Lindsay, late Reader in Indian Law in the University of Oxford, begins with conditions at the establishment of British ascendancy: conquest of Bengal 1757; grant of the Diwani 1765 (fiscal and civil administration of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa, including civil justice); seven years’ delay before the Company assumed the duties. The chapter traces English-rule influences on Indian legal institutions from that starting point.
Chapter IV — Education (J. R. Cunningham)
Cunningham, formerly Director of Public Instruction, Assam, opens from India’s ancient culture and Trevelyan (1838): Western learning as repayment of Europe’s debt to Asia, sciences “cradled in the East and brought to maturity in the West.” Sanskrit already fixed; the “new dispensation” of English education is the subject. Foundations of the Western educational system in India.
Chapter V — The Press (W. C. Wordsworth)
Wordsworth (Director and Assistant Editor of the Statesman, Calcutta and Delhi; formerly Indian Educational Service): India had no Press in the proper sense until the last quarter of the eighteenth century, but older publicity — Asokan pillars, Kalighat pictures, Mughal written news-sheets even for Aurangzeb’s common soldiers. The chapter follows the rise of the modern newspaper under British rule.
Chapter VI — Mechanism and Transport (L. S. S. O’Malley)
Indian genius characterized as more introspective than practical: laws of thought and purification of the soul over mastery of physical forces; mathematics, astronomy, and medicine known early but without the later Western mechanical transformation. The chapter treats the introduction of Western mechanism and transport (railways, telegraphs, and related plant) as a distinct phase of impact.
Chapter VII — Economic Development (Vera Anstey)
Anstey (D.Sc. Econ., London) sets two extreme opinions: British rule as the engine of economic strides versus imperial interests, financial burdens, inappropriate institutions, pressure on the land, drain of wealth, and mass poverty. Critics themselves split between those who accept Western economic ideals and those who do not. The chapter surveys economic development under Western contact and British rule between those poles.
Chapter VIII — The Christian Ethic and India (A. I. Mayhew)
Mayhew: Christian influence since British rule began has been direct (missions) and indirect (administration, education, literature, and mode of life of a civilization owing much to Christian thought). Direct influence is comparatively easy to estimate; indirect influence requires a prior account of how far that civilization depends on distinctively Christian strength. The chapter examines both.
Chapter IX — Hinduism and the West (Sir S. Radhakrishnan)
Radhakrishnan (Spalding Professor of Eastern Religions and Ethics, Oxford): India as home of a civilization as ancient in origins as Egyptian or Sumerian, still functioning for nearly a fifth of the world’s population; saints, sages, poets, philosophers, artists, statesmen; Buddhism, Jainism, Sikhism; cultural unity without which India would be a mere geographical expression. The chapter treats Hinduism’s encounter with the West.
Chapter X — The Hindu Social System (L. S. S. O’Malley)
Two distinctive characteristics versus Western countries: intimate connexion with religion, and a system of groups rather than a synthesis of individuals. Socio-religious order; Śāstras believed of divine origin and still appealed to as ultimate authority though most Hindus know little of their contents and the society they describe has long ceased to exist. Cardinal institutions consecrated by religion; caste treated as the core.
Chapter XI — Muslim Culture and Religious Thought (A. Yusuf Ali)
Yusuf Ali: Indian Muslims stand on a different footing from their Hindu fellow-citizens — historical causes, sociological structure, and different religious ideals. Islam is a world religion in intimate contact from its origin with Christianity and Judaism, and with Greek and Roman ideas; earliest systematic expositions clothed in methods of the schools of Alexandria. The chapter treats Muslim culture and religious thought under Western interaction.
Chapter XII — Primitive Tribes (J. H. Hutton)
Hutton (Professor of Social Anthropology, Cambridge): before Western contacts can be weighed, the pre-British position of primitive tribes must be formed. Tribes fade into castes, generally depressed castes, without a clear line; waves of invasion drove defeated peoples into forests and hills; cultural conquests of Hinduism and Buddhism affected the plains. The chapter then considers Western contact with those tribes.
Chapter XIII — The Progress of Women (Mrs. H. Gray)
Gray: Western impact brought changes more fundamental for women than for men. To men, a new conception of the world; to women, slowly but potently, a new conception of themselves — revaluation as human beings in a new social order. “Let us go back to the Vedas,” cry the women, to days of equality in religion, marriage, property, and service of the State. The chapter traces that revaluation.
Chapter XIV — Literature and Drama (six vernaculars)
Six commissioned sketches, not a complete Indian literature:

Bengali (J. C. Ghosh, Oxford) — beginnings about the eleventh century; middle period fourteenth/fifteenth; modern period from 1800 and Fort William College, Calcutta. Nineteenth century as the period of Western influence mainly through English education; literature after 1800 larger in bulk than the preceding nine or ten centuries.
Hindi (Rao Raja Shyam Behari Misra and Rai Bahadur Sukhdeo Behari Misra).
Marathi (V. P. Dandekar, Baroda College).
Tamil (S. S. Bharati, formerly Annamalai University).
Telugu (Vidwan G. J. Somayaji, Andhra University).
Urdu (Sir Abdul Qadir).

Meston notes the field was confined to these six for difficulty of choice if widened.
Chapter XV — Indian Influence on the West (H. G. Rawlinson)
Rawlinson: cultural interactions go back to remote times. Despite silence of classical authors, Greek thought from Pythagoras to Plato is argued to show Hindu parallels; the link is the Persian Empire (Darius I and Scylax of Caryanda on the Indus, 517 B.C.); Alexander in the Punjab 327 B.C.; Megasthenes at Pataliputra. The chapter follows Indian influence westward from antiquity through later European reception.
Chapter XVI — General Survey (L. S. S. O’Malley)
Opens under the heading Contacts: first Western contacts as mere juxtaposition — scattered coastal settlements and inland trading posts; primary object trade, depending on mutual confidence. Acquisition of territorial sovereignty put relations on a different footing: domination, closer contact, numbers at first utterly inadequate, paucity and want of administrative experience. The long closing survey draws the specialist chapters together.
Notes for later extraction
Entity and event pages await a Proceed batch. Natural first filings from this source: Vasco da Gama / Calicut 1498; Diwani 1765; Fort William College; Macaulay/Trevelyan education policy; caste and the Śāstras; Chatham House / O’Malley as editorial frame. Companion sources for Company–Crown India will sit beside this symposium as they are added.

sources/russell-short-history-eic.title: Francis Russell — A Short History of the East India Company (1793)
sources/russell-short-history-eic.content:
A Short History of the East India Company (Russell, 1793)
A second-edition London pamphlet, attributed to Francis Russell, written as Parliament prepared to renew the East India Company’s exclusive trade (term ending 1794): origin of the old and new companies, India-House 3 per cent annuities, purchased versus conquered forts, expenses of conquest, chartered rights, the “monopoly” charge, foreign rivals, trade and shipping, profits, the Company as sovereign and merchant, objections to innovation, a regulated opening for private merchants, then a postscript, a law discussion of Masulipatam and the Northern Circars, four-year sales figures, and an abridgment of the 1793 Act.
Summary
Title-page (OCR): A Short History of the East India Company: exhibiting a state of their affairs, abroad and at home, political and commercial; the nature and magnitude of their commerce, and its relative connection with the government and revenues of India; and a discussion on the question of right to the conquered territories in India; also remarks on the danger and impolicy of innovation, and the practical means of ensuring all the good effects of a free trade to the manufacturers of Great Britain and Ireland, by matter of regulation, without disturbing the established system. The second edition, with some additions. To which is added, an abridgment of the new act. London: John Sewell, Cornhill, and John Debrett, Piccadilly, 1793. NYPL copy (Astor, Lenox and Tilden Foundations, 1910), marked Russell, Copy 2. Wrapper/OCLC 40214405 names Francis Russell.
The introduction presents the tract as information for senators on the eve of a “most serious investigation” of the India and China trade. The second edition reprints a well-received first; a new section answers official doubt of the editor’s claim (ch. III) that the Company has exclusive property and revenue of the five Northern Circars.
The argument throughout is that exclusive joint-stock trade rests on parliamentary compact and purchase, not mere prerogative; that territorial revenues have not yet reimbursed conquest debts; that “chartered monopoly” is a popular odium; that a fully open trade would endanger the political chain with India; and that private merchants can be given the benefits of the trade by regulation (especially cheaper freight) without breaking the system. Postscript (dated as in the former edition, February 1793): the Company’s published statement of probable net surplus of territorial revenues and trade profits in profound peace. Additional ch. XV: Crown versus Company at law over Masulipatam and the Northern Circars, as the 1781 compact nears expiry and ministers offer propositions for continuing government and a new partition of surplus. Closing: four years of India/China sales, duties, exports, drawbacks; abridgment of the Act settling government and trade and appropriating territorial revenues and profits of trade (Charter Act 1793).
Source
Russell, Francis. A Short History of the East India Company … 2nd ed., with additions and an abridgment of the new Act. London: John Sewell and John Debrett, 1793. Local file: Anna’s Archive ZIP of 124 NYPL page OCR texts (33433020587584/00000001.txt … 00000124.txt).
Full raw text concatenated at raw.txt (264,562 bytes; 4,783 lines; sha256 f31be4207cd61709449215b2e10c20c63eec0cd02e7b141c400509fbc040739a). OCR medium: long-s rendered as f, broken hyphenation, running headers, TOC chapter numbers split across lines, some headings recovered as “CHAPTER” on a line after the numeral. Page markers in the extract are ZIP sequence numbers; printed pagination in the contents runs introduction p. 1 through the Act abridgment p. 75.
Contents
Printed contents: Introduction; I Origin of the Old and New Companies, with their Union; II Origin of the 3 per cent. annuities transferrable at the India House; III Forts, factories, and territories (purchase vs conquest); IV Expenses of the Indian conquests; V Permanent and temporary rights; VI How far “chartered monopoly” applies; VII Former plans for varying the trade; VIII Present state of foreign countries’ trade with India and China; IX Returns of trade before and after territorial acquisition; debts and claims on the public; X Nature and extent of trade and shipping; XI Profits of trade; XII Company as sovereigns and merchants; XIII Recapitulation, parliamentary objections, innovation; XIV Practical means for private merchants without disturbing the system; Postscript; Additional ch. XV (territories; Crown vs Company); Account of imports sold in the last four years; Abridgment of the new Act.
Introduction
Liberty of the press as the means by which practical knowledge reaches Parliament. The editor’s “particular situation and line of life” as his warrant for setting out the India and China trade. Object: a connected brief of origin and progress of the trade and companies before the present state. Second edition: added section on the Northern Circars after the third chapter’s opinion was questioned in high official situations.
Chapter I — Origin of the Old and New Companies, with their Union
Sea passage to India not discovered until the later fifteenth century; first successful English incorporation The London East India Company, charter 31 December 1600. Factories in India and Persia; Crown charters without parliamentary sanction until after the Restoration. Interlopers; 1693 default on a duty voiding charters; revival on three years’ notice; 1698 Act borrowing two millions at 8 per cent. and incorporating a General Society and The English East India Company; Old Company buys into the loan; union 1702, confirmed under Godolphin 1708. Warehouses, shipping, settlements (including Bombay and St Helena) vest in the United Company. General Society’s separate traders shrink to £7,000 then absorbed. Footnotes list forts (Mazagon, Mahim, Fort St George, Fort William, Bombay, St Helena, &c.) and factories (Surat, Agra, Cossimbuzar, Dacca, Hugli, Patna, &c.).
Chapter II — 3 per cent. annuities at the India House
Public debt of £4,200,000 to the Company; interest reduced in 1750 to 3 per cent., £126,000 a year. Salt and stamp duties as securities. Premium of £200,000 and interest cuts for extensions of exclusive trade; 1744 loan of one million at 3 per cent. (raised on bonds, not added to dividend capital of £3,200,000). Last renewal 1781 (21 Geo. III c. 65): exclusive trade to 1794 for £400,000 in discharge of public claims before 1 March 1781; after 8 per cent. dividend, surplus of net trade and revenues three-fourths to the Public, one-fourth to the Company — no such surplus yet because of Indian war debts. Compulsory tea stock (1784) and new subscriptions to five millions (1786, 1789).
Chapter III — Forts, factories, and territories (purchase vs conquest)
Before suggesting future trade regulations, distinguish possessions held in perpetuity from those claimed by the public. Purchase versus conquest; Clive-era military acquisitions; Commons resolution 1773 that acquisitions under military force or treaty belong to the State; earlier royal licence to the Company to cede conquests except European settlements.
Chapter IV — Expenses of the Indian conquests
Answer to the claim that territorial revenues and commercial funds are so blended that conquest cost cannot be known, and receipts may be set against payments forever. Russell: if revenues stayed with the Company until debts were cleared, that close might be acceptable; as things stand, land revenues have fallen short of reimbursing territorial disbursements by the full amount of debts abroad and at home (current commercial debts excepted). Method: an account at home, since remittances come only through investments.
Chapter V — Permanent and temporary rights
Against the “prevailing error” that corporate capacity, joint-stock trade, and chartered rights all determine in 1794 unless renewed. Distinguishes rights that need renewal from those that stand in the way of laying the trade open.
Chapter VI — “Chartered monopoly”
The phrase is meant to excite popular odium. Old Company held exclusive trade by voluntary Crown grant on prerogative; the present Company holds by purchase from the Public on parliamentary compact. King William’s charter of incorporation is distinguished from those purchased rights.
Chapter VII — Former plans for varying the trade
No grave proposal to throw the trade wholly open to chance. Serious alternatives were a Regulated Open Company (every merchant trades on his own stock under company regulation): the 1600 company and the General Society both grew into joint-stock companies. Interlopers, Mogul resentment, five years’ interruption, a king’s ship and proclamation to force interlopers under Company jurisdiction.
Chapter VIII — Foreign countries’ trade with India and China
Portuguese, Spaniards, French, Danes, Dutch: privileges of free trade and factories. French, Danes, Dutch mostly by companies like England’s; Portuguese by houses and individuals; Spanish trade dwindled; Swedish company chiefly China, no continental settlements. Commutation Act 1784 and lower tea duties: Company undersells smugglers via Ostend, Dunkirk; Swedish, Danish, Embden companies almost annihilated; Trieste Company stopped. Dutch spice monopoly (pepper excepted); distress after the American-war rupture with England; loans from the States General. French failures; present French company buys from the English Company. Private adventurers from Sweden, Denmark, Ostend, France, Portugal, America as a caution against small-capital Asiatic speculation.
Chapter IX — Trade returns before and after territory; debts; indemnification
Before 1757, sale amount of imports rarely exceeded two millions in a year. Investments from exports, bullion, and servants’ bills on London. Acquisition of territories changes exports and imports; present debts; claims on the public for expenses of acquiring and preserving conquered provinces.
Chapter X — Nature and extent of trade and shipping
Exports: House of Commons has printed three Directors’ reports to the Board of Commerce, reprinted by the Company; Russell recites them rather than recompute species, quantities, and values. Shipping employed in the India and China trade.
Chapter XI — Profits of trade
Published accounts do not separate profit and loss on export trade: merchandise blended with military stores; merchandise charges blended with recruits, gratuities, pensions, law. About 1780, export trade and duty on private trade cleared a medium profit equal to £2 12s. 6d. per cent. a year on the old capital of £3,200,000; China export profits computed at £65,000 a year; India exports doubted to yield real profit. Import sales 1791–93: produce exceeds invoice plus customs, freight, and charges.
Chapter XII — Sovereigns and merchants
Compact of 1781: after 8 per cent. dividend, surplus three-fourths public, one-fourth Company. War and increased civil and military establishments 1779–82 made those funds deficient. In 1783 the Public agreed to forgo participation until certain debts were discharged.
Chapter XIII — Recapitulation; parliamentary objections; innovation
Company threatened with serious opposition to exclusive trade. Members of the legislature and the public need the Company’s acknowledged rights and how they are upheld. Circumspection before any change of system that might lose or divert this branch of British commerce (employment, revenues, re-export carrying trade, Eastern articles at reasonable prices).
Chapter XIV — Practical means without disturbing the system
Freight: advancement of export and import depends on conveyance at a reasonable rate, long fruitlessly attempted, so manufacturers and merchants will adventure on their own risk. Directors will find it hard to persuade of present freight rates. Object: private merchant and public get the ultimate benefits inside exclusive limits without endangering the political connection with India.
Postscript (February 1793, as in the former edition)
Since the sheets went to press, the Company has published a statement of probable net annual surplus of territorial revenues in India and profits on trade in profound peace — not a medium of former actual receipts and disbursements.
Additional Chapter XV — Masulipatam and the Northern Circars
Question as between the Crown and the Company of the town, port, and district of Masulipatam and of the Northern Circars on the Coromandel coast. 1781 compact near expiry; ministers offer propositions to continue the system of government and a new partition of surplus.
Account of imports (last four years)
India and China goods sold at the Company’s sales; duties and customs; amount exported each year; drawbacks on exportation.
Abridgment of the new Act
Act for settling the government and trade of India, and for the appropriation of the territorial revenues and profits of trade (the 1793 charter legislation).
Notes for later extraction
Pair with malcolm-life-of-clive-vol1–malcolm-life-of-clive-vol3 for the conquests this pamphlet costs and defends, and with Whyte/O’Malley for later Company-to-Crown narrative. Natural filings: London vs English EIC union 1702/1708; 1781 compact; Diwani vs “acquisitions belong to the State” (1773); Northern Circars; Commutation Act 1784; Charter Act 1793. Entity/event pages await Proceed.

sources/temple-india-in-1880.title: Sir Richard Temple — India in 1880 (3rd ed., 1881)
sources/temple-india-in-1880.content:
India in 1880 (Temple, 1881)
Sir Richard Temple, Bart., G.C.S.I., C.I.E., D.C.L. (1826–1902), late Governor of Bombay, Lieutenant-Governor of Bengal, and Finance Minister of India. John Murray, Albemarle Street; third edition, 1881 (first issued December 1880). Dedicated, with permission, to the Prince of Wales in memory of the Indian visit. Michigan copy (39015067228182).
Completeness
Complete as a single volume.

Title-page THIRD EDITION. WITH TWO MAPS. 568 OCR leaves. Prefaces (third edition, April 1882 at The Nash, Kempsey; first preface December 1880); twenty-seven chapters; index.
Closer is the finance chapter and index; no further volumes advertised.

Summary
Temple’s thirty-year tour of the empire as a dispassionate survey for English readers who ask about India — travellers, missionaries, economists, statesmen. Nature and art; Covenanted Civil Service and planters; Native States as a safety-valve; population, wealth, and remittances; mental/moral progress and the vernacular press; education since 1854; missions; law and “over-legislation”; thagi, sati, police, prisons; land tax and tenures; revenues (salt, opium, piece-goods duties); canals, railways, roads; forests and industry; commerce and the “drain”; sanitation; famines of 1874 and 1877; Asiatic Society and surveys; sport; navy and marine; the army; foreign relations (Aden to Merv, Herat, Candahar); finance and loss by exchange. Third-edition preface answers charges of vagueness and optimism, lists troubles (discontent, famine recurrence, Russian approach), and notes Afghan war paid without new debt and a surplus after salt/customs cuts.
Source
Temple, Sir Richard. India in 1880. Third edition. With two maps. London: John Murray, Albemarle Street. 1881. Printed by William Clowes and Sons. OCLC 5867054. Local file: Anna’s Archive ZIP hash 0662413bdb14358e4d8bc1709cfe39e2.
Full raw text concatenated at raw.txt (1,174,808 bytes; 25,454 lines; sha256 76b9cf07e674d75aa921bc1c3ebed108c24006b13b617ee81269c28896e407d5). OCR medium.
Contents
Twenty-seven chapters; maps (India; detail sheets in the ZIP as image OCR).
Chapter I — Claims of India on the continuous attention of England
England must watch a changeful dependency. Survey of India in 1880 for travellers and sportsmen, art and science, missions, public affairs, economists and statesmen.
Chapter II — Objects of beauty in nature
Travel facilities; rains; north vs south of the “backbone” ranges; hill stations; Himalayan views; rivers, marble rocks, cascades, snow peaks, Kashmir; costumes of the races. Aimed at intending travellers (with ch. III and XXIII).
Chapter III — Objects of beauty in art
British-period views at Bombay, Calcutta, railways; churches; Buddhist caves and frescoes; Jain sacred mountains; Hindu temples and hill forts; Mughal work — largest dome, city of the dead, Akbar, Delhi Jama Masjid, Pearl Mosque, Taj Mahal.
Chapter IV — European classes, official and non-official
Covenanted Civil Service after competition; civil duties; historic names; military officers in civil/political employ; medical, engineers, clergy and prelates; uncovenanted and East-Indian officers; mercantile firms, chambers; indigo, tea, coffee; Anglo-Indian press.
Chapter V — Native States
Relations with the paramount power; loyalty in the Mutiny; Star of India; Imperial Assemblage at Delhi; Prince of Wales’s visit. Political value of the States; education of young princes; administration and armies. Nizam, Jammu and Kashmir, protected Sikhs, Rajputs, Sindia/Holkar/Gaekwar, Bhopal, Travancore, Deccan, Mysore, Nepal, Khelat; eminent Native statesmen.
Chapter VI — Material progress of the Natives
Census and growth; expansion of cultivation; cultivable waste; emigration to colonies; food supply; wealth under British rule; remittances to England; English capital; cattle; why India is poorer than the West; the poor; industry; general condition. Preface gloss: land can feed the added numbers; wealth rising and fairly diffused except the humblest.
Chapter VII — Mental and moral progress of the Natives
Effects on peasantry, aboriginal tribes, Muhammadans, Parsis, nobility, landlords, traders, priesthood, educated classes (mind, morals, belief, loyalty, aspirations); munificence; science; vernacular press and drama; Natives in the services and professions; visits to England; general temper. Preface lists discontents: Mutiny-era classes, Muhammadan fanaticism, decayed aristocracy, Hindu priesthood, Sikhism, educated aspirations, vernacular press.
Chapter VIII — National education
1854 policy; scholars vs population; finance; primary and village masters; middle schools; want of technical instruction; normal schools; vernacular literature; universities and affiliated colleges; Native graduates; medicine, engineering, science degrees, agriculture, art schools; ethics; female education and zenana missions; European and East-Indian children.
Chapter IX — Religious establishments and missions
State Church; Native rulers’ endowments partly maintained; Portuguese establishments; government attitude; missions in Native States; Roman Catholic and Protestant work; statistics; high authorities in favour; Native Christians and a Native Church; Oxford/Cambridge missions; moral effect. Preface: large success claimed, decisive influence for good.
Chapter X — Law and legislation
Parliamentary constitution of the government; sacred Hindu and Muhammadan law; English law; legislative councils; London Law Commission; civil courts and High Courts; peasant-debt legislation; arbitration; patriarchal and non-regulation systems; answer to over-legislation; need of continuity.
Chapter XI — Crime, police and prisons
Character of crime; thagi repressed; sati suppressed; female infanticide; marriage-expense regulation; Deccan dacoity; gypsy tribes; riots; Penal Code and procedure; reorganized police; village police; arms; prisons, reformatories, Port Blair. Preface: police faults remain; prison mortality not rare.
Chapter XII — Land-tax and landed tenures
Tax as rent-share and produce percentage; field survey and record of rights; property in land created or recognised; fee-simple Europeans; permanent settlement; northern village communities; Madras/Bombay tenures; village officers; indebted peasant proprietors; occupancy tenants vs tenants at will. Preface: settlement and recognition of property a perpetual boon; occupancy protected, tenants-at-will not yet.
Chapter XIII — Revenues
Land revenue rates; tributes; excise; assessed taxes; customs; abolition of import duties on English piece goods suggested; salt tax; English salt; opium revenue and moral objections answered; stamps; local/municipal taxes; new taxes deprecated.
Chapter XIV — Canals and irrigation
Navigation and irrigation; wells; Native works; British canals in Hindustan, Punjab, Bihar, Orissa, Godavari/Kistna deltas, Tanjore, Tungabhadra, Sind; Madras/Bombay tanks; water-rent; financial returns; famine value.
Chapter XV — Railways and electric telegraphs
Dalhousie’s design; Calcutta–NW frontier, Calcutta–Bombay, Bombay–Madras, Lahore–Karachi; projected Candahar; other lines; Guaranteed vs State; Native capital; gauges; war and famine; telegraph to England and abroad.
Chapter XVI — Roads and embankments
Native vs British roads; trunk lines; bridging and metalling; pack-bullocks to carts; embankments in Bengal, Bihar, Orissa, Indus valley.
Chapter XVII — Products, natural, agricultural and industrial
Tea, coffee, tobacco, cinchona, cotton (mills and factory legislation), jute; forests — past destruction, conservancy, climate, pasturage, communal forests, Forest Department; coal, iron, gold, gems; industrial arts and exhibitions; danger of stifling Native art-genius with misapplied European ideas.
Chapter XVIII — Commerce, external and internal
East-Indiamen, Green’s ships, P&O, Suez Canal; trade with Europe, US, Mauritius; shipping mostly British; coasting; balance of trade; Home remittances; export value; food supply; internal trade and price equalization. Preface: “drain” allegations controverted.
Chapter XIX — Public health and sanitation
Sanitary department; vital statistics; hygiene teaching; urban water-works; conservancy and sewage; lodging-houses; village dwellings; food; smallpox and vaccination; contagious diseases; hospitals.
Chapter XX — Famine
Under Native and British rule; Bihar/Bengal 1874; Madras/Bombay 1877; English and Indian charity; mortality; railways; precautions — stop wandering, relief works, village inspection, relief houses; peasantry not demoralized; private food supply.
Chapter XXI — Learned research
Orientalist tradition; historic fiction; civil, political, military history; biographies; ethnology; travel beyond the Indus; Asiatic Society of Bengal; Bombay RAS; Archaeological Survey; preservation of monuments.
Chapter XXII — Physical science
Great Trigonometrical and topographical surveys; Madras observatory; meteorology; botanic gardens; Geological Survey; museum; ornithology; zoos; Basevi and Stoliczka; pisciculture; agricultural department, model farms; veterinary art.
Chapter XXIII — Wild animals and sports
Boar, tiger, man-eater, panther, cheetah, bear, elephant, bison, rhinoceros, alligator, Himalayan ibex and Ovis Ammon; Anglo-Indian sporting literature.
Chapter XXIV — Navy and marine
Early enterprise and piracy; Indian Navy abolished; Admiralty arrangement; Persian Gulf; harbour defence; steam companies; Indian Marine; surveys and tides; wrecks; Native passenger ships; Calcutta, Hughli pilots, cyclones; Madras pier; dockyards; Bombay wet dock; Karachi; lighthouses.
Chapter XXV — The army
European soldier (short service, volunteers); Native armies of the three Presidencies; castes and tribes; fidelity’s basis; recruiting difficulty; Native and European officers; staff corps; cavalry, ordnance, commissariat, transport; established strength. Preface: do not reduce fighting strength.
Chapter XXVI — Foreign relations
Aden, Arabia, Socotra, Muscat, Persian Gulf, Mesopotamia, Malacca, Ava, China, Tibet, Yarkand; NW frontier and Afghanistan; opinion on Russia; Kokand, Bukhara, Khiva; Badakhshan and Balkh; Persia and Herat; Russian advance on Merv; Khyber, Kurram, Pishin, Candahar. Third-edition note: Askabad–Serakhs line, Caspian railway, Turkomans subdued, Herat nearer.
Chapter XXVII — Finance
Budget published in India; elasticity doubts; military and civil cost; provincial services; European vs Native agency; guaranteed and State railways; irrigation outlay and famine results; loss by exchange; gold-standard talk; debt; equilibrium; audit; paper currency; mints; savings-banks; Presidency banks; cash balances. Preface: Afghan war paid from revenues and English £5m help without new debt; surplus after tax cuts; population +13 million in ten years despite famine deaths.
Notes

Written at the hinge between Lytton and Ripon; pairs with wolf-life-of-ripon-vol2 for the same years from a Bombay/Bengal/Finance official’s desk.
Contemporary-lens reading: Temple answers the “drain,” opium morals, and Russian scare while listing enough dangers to deny the charge of mere optimism.
Maps are present as image leaves in the OCR set; text extract does not render them.

sources/wolf-life-of-ripon-vol1.title: Lucien Wolf — Life of the First Marquess of Ripon, Vol. I (1921)
sources/wolf-life-of-ripon-vol1.content:
Life of the First Marquess of Ripon, Vol. I (Wolf, 1921)
Lucien Wolf (1857–1930). Two volumes, John Murray, 1921. This file is Vol. I. Official life, from family papers at the request of Sir Henry Primrose and the executors. Preface (Gray’s Inn, September 1921): delay from Wolf’s eyesight and the War; C. E. Baines of the India Office digested the viceroyalty papers (used mainly in Vol. II); conversion chapter by Father Sebastian Bowden.
Completeness
Complete as Volume I of two. Not the complete Life.

Title-page IN TWO VOLUMES / VOL. I. 386 OCR leaves, Internet Archive ark+=13960=t3513x75c.
Books I–III, chs I–XIII, plus Bowden’s supplementary chapter on the 1874 conversion. Closer is Ripon’s last sacraments (in Bowden’s chapter), then Hazell, Watson and Viney imprint.
The Indian Viceroyalty (1880–84) is not narrated here; the volume ends with Gladstone making him a Catholic Viceroy. Continues in Vol. II.

Summary
George Frederick Samuel Robinson is born 24 October 1827 in Downing Street while his father, Lord Goderich, is Premier after Canning; a postscript about the baby’s health helps wreck the cabinet. Wolf’s official life, written from family papers for the executors, treats him as a “noble democrat”: Christian Socialist pamphlet, Hull unseated for bribery, Huddersfield, Crimea fire-eater, 1857–58 Indian apprenticeship in the Commons (Mutiny, Ellenborough vs “Clemency Canning,” civil service and native army), Under-Secretary then Secretary for War (Herbert, Nightingale, Cardwell’s prelude), Secretary for India with Lawrence, Lord President (Forster’s Education Act, Washington / Alabama claims, Marquessate), resignation 1873, conversion to Rome 1874 against Gladstone’s Vatican Decrees, return in 1880 as Gladstone’s Catholic Viceroy. The viceroyalty itself is Vol. II.
Source
Wolf, Lucien. Life of the First Marquess of Ripon, K.G., P.C., G.C.S.I., D.C.L., etc. With illustrations. In two volumes. Volume I. London: John Murray, Albemarle Street, W. 1921. OCLC 384232. Local file: Anna’s Archive ZIP hash 294177b159b9be0078d4d03d44c7e396.
Full raw text concatenated at raw.txt (682,732 bytes; 16,816 lines; sha256 40a65bdb4cff583522be3d09469ea06a706ebdc544254305e3d6d045c319d872). OCR medium.
Contents
Printed contents: Book I chs I–III; Book II chs IV–VIII; Book III chs IX–XIII; supplementary chapter on conversion.
Book I — The noble democrat
Chapter I — Heredity and the fairy godmother (1827)
Times, 27 October 1827: Lady Goderich delivered of a son at the Premier’s house in Downing Street, only child after the death of a daughter. Wolf’s “fairy godmother” is the ministerial purple plus the cradle-anxieties that help unmake the cabinet before the boy is six weeks old. After Canning’s death (August 1827) the King wants a Premier he can manage: Goderich, amiable, shrewd, easily unnerved. Whigs press Lord Holland; the King foists Herries; Navarino splits Huskisson and Herries. Goderich, after agreeing a threat of resignation with Lansdowne and Huskisson, adds a postscript no colleague sees: domestic circumstances affecting “one most dear to him.” The baby is christened George Frederick Samuel (Hannah’s prayer). Robinsons of Newby: William of York in the Hamburg kersey trade, Lord Mayor, interloper against the Steelyard; Fountains Abbey romance; “Prosperity Robinson”; Ripon peerage; a Cromwellian strain the later Marquess still hugged at eighty (“If I had to write this over again I should not alter a word”). Wolf’s point: Radicalism and Whig acres, ultramontanism and “pledge of moderation,” live in the same man.
Chapter II — “The duty of the age” (1852)
Ripon tells Sir Bruce Seton he did well without a public school: home education late and unmethodical; he taught himself writing from discarded envelopes. Nocton (Hobart/Buckinghamshire; hall burnt 1834; foundation-stone 1841) and squire-parsons (Curtois, Thirkill White): muscular Christianity, shooting, fishing, entomology, and a secretive habit of reading himself into convictions. 1848; Christian Socialism with Kingsley, Maurice, Hughes; marriage; engineers’ strike. A political pamphlet indicts aristocracy as failing “the duty of the age”; Kingsley backs it, Maurice criticizes; Goderich will not recant. The “higher man” is his answer to class war: landowners who work, not palaver.
Chapter III — The fallen prophet (1852–1853)
Honeymoon year; son Oliver (“Noll”) born January 1852, named for the Protector. Letters to Hughes from Wrest and Ollerton: carp, beetles, dull sermons, good beer. Parliamentary candidature; elected for Hull; a bribery scandal unseats him; victory at Huddersfield. Disillusionment: the prophet of Christian Socialism meets election agents and the “Palaver.”
Book II — Six years in the Commons
Chapter IV — Mumps and dumps (1853)
Goderich sits only six years (from age 26) and still makes a name, while loathing the House’s “perpetual jaw.” Letters to Hughes: he looks forward to the Lords and the “grand work” of a landowner; no faith in the Commons; “soul-destroying atmosphere” even in 1855. Goderichites; Lancashire strikes; franchise; boards of conciliation; co-partnership. Fragmentary Wild Oats is the scrapbook of this cooling Socialism turning into Whig paternalism.
Chapter V — A man of war (1853–1856)
Anglo-French war with Russia, March 1854, finds him with the fire-eaters. Kimberley later: “a man of war from his youth.” At home he has become apostle of peace and co-operation; in foreign politics he is still 1789 Jacobin and will not be kind to despots. He attacks the Peace Society for denouncing all war and all soldiers (Mammon-worship, denial of national life). Crimea: case against Russia, proposed German alliance, Alma, a national army, an offer of office, a parliamentary mistake, the problem of peace, fall of Kars, end of the war.
Chapter VI — The Indian apprenticeship (1857–1858)
Peace does not heal Palmerston’s enemies. The “fortuitous concourse of atoms” (Tories, Peelites, Whigs, Manchester) try to upset him; China debate, 3 March 1857, majority of 16 against the government; Palmerston dissolves and comes back with 85. Cobden, Bright, Gibson, Miall, Layard out; Goderich survives by moving to the West Riding (Forster working for him; Cobden takes Huddersfield and is crushed). Then the Mutiny. Ellis of Nagpore; “Well done, Pam!” Ellenborough’s bill and an Indian Council; “Clemency Canning”; Goderich vs Ellenborough. A scheme of reform: civil service, native army. This is Commons India after the Company, not the later viceroyalty.
Chapter VII — Surrender to Palmerston (1855–1859)
Reputation reaches Ellis in Nagpore and an American visitor who wants to see the man from the speeches. Early relations with Gladstone; “ministrable”; Lady Palmerston’s views. Conspiracy to Murder bill (Orsini): revenge of the atoms; Goderich’s vote is a mental struggle. Views on reform. He takes Under-Secretary for War — the surrender of the chapter title: office under the Dictator he had helped to harry.
Chapter VIII — Off the stage (1852–1859)
Private life against the palaver: religious consolation, holidays, Tom Hughes in Wales, a composite letter, the parson and the “Lord,” Italy, seaside lodgings, a trio of friends, the Working Men’s College. Light and shade before Pall Mall swallows him.
Book III — In and out of office
Chapter IX — Reforming the War Office (1859–1863)
Palmerston–Russell army years as the start of the line that runs through Cardwell (1870) to Esher and Haldane. Sidney Herbert and Under-Secretary de Grey; Forster expects much; Mansfield writes from Simla under Clyde that he is glad de Grey is in the War Department. Chaos in Pall Mall; China war; de Grey’s scheme; a spell at the India Office; Herbert dies; back to Pall Mall. Reforms actually accomplished; Volunteer movement; first Easter Monday review; Hughes’s report. High hopes not fully realized — not Herbert’s or de Grey’s fault.
Chapter X — In the Cabinet (1863–1866)
Cornewall Lewis dies 13 April 1863. Clarendon’s tribute; Gladstone still wants the War Secretary in the Commons and thinks de Grey a militarist spendthrift; Florence Nightingale pushes de Grey for her schemes. He becomes Secretary for War. Crawley scandal; tampering with the press; colonial garrisons; defences of Canada; Schleswig-Holstein (war and economy, Queen’s queries, desertion of Denmark). Palmerston dies; reconstruction; outstanding War Office reforms; Secretary for India; de Grey and Lawrence.
Chapter XI — The Lord President (1868–1873)
Derby–Disraeli after Russell (June 1866): “extra dances” with the extreme left; Lowe on two parties bidding for Demos; Carlyle’s “Shooting Niagara.” Gladstone’s new cabinet; compromises with Tories; university tests; K.G. and D.C.L. Education: Forster’s Elementary Education Act and church schools. American grievances; plan of settlement; mission to Washington; Alabama claims; the crux; a row in the cabinet; Washington Treaty signed; created a Marquess.
Chapter XII — Discords and a rupture (1871–1873)
Education Act and Washington Treaty both still fighting. Indirect claims (Sumner’s invention: Britain responsible for prolonging the Civil War, shipping decline, insurance — Gladstone says damages might exceed the National Debt) were thought excluded; they return. Hamilton Fish’s tactics; talk in Harley Street; additional article; Ripon against the cabinet; Queen’s intervention; debate in the Lords; Granville’s bombshell; comedy at Geneva. Chamberlain and the pauper child. County franchise; Ripon resigns (1873). Salisbury’s sympathy; alone with Newman — the religious hinge of the next chapter.
Chapter XIII — From King Solomon’s throne to the Pope’s footstool (1874–1880)
1874 Liberal landslide out; Disraeli in; Public Worship Regulation Act; Bismarck’s Kulturkampf; Gladstone to Döllinger then the Vatican Decrees. Early September: Ripon’s secession to Rome, received as a Protestant storm. Career in Freemasonry dropped. Friends’ attitude; Gladstone’s explosion; Ripon’s remonstrance (decrees misinterpreted); “a personal matter”; satisfactory explanations; silence and patience. Catholics and party politics. Return; Gladstone premier again; a Catholic Viceroy — the appointment that opens Vol. II.
Supplementary chapter — Lord Ripon’s conversion (1874) (Father Sebastian Bowden, London Oratory)
Earlier impressions via Father Donald Skrimshire: delicate Evangelical boy; at 17 finds an old breviary in a Ripon bookshop; office discontinued; awakened by the brigand-murder of brother-in-law Frederick Vyner in Greece (April 1870); first Mass in England at St George’s, Southwark. Four more years an Anglican. Correspondence: doubts, Syllabus, Church and liberalism, the gulf crossed, obedience to the Pope, points of doctrine, prayer and distractions, moral courage. Letters from old friends: grief, no blame. Apostolic benediction; Manning. Closer of the volume is the death-bed (anticipating 1909): Studley chapel to Our Lady of Fountains; last sacraments from Father Levick; Pius IX’s crucifix.
Notes

Two-volume official life. Vol. II (viceroyalty and after) is wolf-life-of-ripon-vol2.
Contemporary-lens reading: Wolf (1921) writes Ripon back up from “political mediocrity” after the War; India in this volume is Mutiny Commons and the India Office, then the appointment of a Catholic Viceroy as the hinge to Vol. II.
Illustrations listed (Herkomer frontispiece, boy, Marchioness, Buckinghamshire, Alabama cartoon) are not in the OCR text files.

sources/wolf-life-of-ripon-vol2.title: Lucien Wolf — Life of the First Marquess of Ripon, Vol. II (1921)
sources/wolf-life-of-ripon-vol2.content:
Life of the First Marquess of Ripon, Vol. II (Wolf, 1921)
Lucien Wolf. Two volumes, John Murray, 1921. This file is Vol. II and completes the Life. Book IV is the Indian Viceroyalty; Book V the elder statesman. University of Wisconsin copy.
Completeness
Complete as Volume II of two. Completes the 1921 Life.

Title-page IN TWO VOLUMES / VOL. II. 456 OCR leaves (folder 89094712510). Continues wolf-life-of-ripon-vol1.
Book IV chs XIV–XXI (1880–84); Book V chs XXII–XXVI (1885–1909); appendices I–IX (Goderich cabinet through Ilbert Bill, imperial preferences, Cromwell/Hampden descent); index covering both volumes.
No “END OF VOL.” line; text runs into index.

Summary
Ripon sails within a fortnight of accepting, into heat Lytton compared to “the furnaces of Nebuchadnezzar,” because India had been Beaconsfield’s glittering theatre and Lytton more Disraelian than Disraeli. Book IV: Afghanistan (Sher Ali, Abdur Rahman, Maiwand, Roberts to Kandahar, evacuate Kandahar / keep Pishin), army and Russia, Baring and tenancy, local self-government, Vernacular Press Act, Ilbert Bill. Book V: Home Rule, Admiralty, colonial preference, Rosebery vs Harcourt vs Campbell-Bannerman, 1906 Education Bill, Morley’s Indian reforms, death 1909.
Source
Wolf, Lucien. Life of the First Marquess of Ripon, K.G., P.C., G.C.S.I., D.C.L., etc. With illustrations. In two volumes. Volume II. London: John Murray, Albemarle Street, W. 1921. OCLC 384232. Local file: Anna’s Archive ZIP hash 3addfc70eeefec681f379604805d6c6a. Wisconsin library stamps.
Full raw text concatenated at raw.txt (804,010 bytes; 19,299 lines; sha256 eafc9a03d9f4c55b9ef2bbfcbc8146a03b9f42fc30543c84d867e8888f5bad32). OCR medium.
Contents
Printed contents: Book IV chs XIV–XXI; Book V chs XXII–XXVI; appendices; index.
Book IV — The Indian Viceroyalty
Chapter XIV — The furnaces of Nebuchadnezzar (1880)
Within a fortnight of accepting he is on the road. The plains, Lytton to Cranbrook, are “hotter than the furnaces of Nebuchadnezzar”; the need at Simla is judged imperative on party grounds as well as Afghan ones. India had been Beaconsfield’s glittering theatre; Lytton, in pose and dream, more Disraelian than his chief (his own fancy: “supremacy of Central Asia and the revenues of a first-class Power”). Immediate recall marks the Liberal victory. Ripon’s health; Gordon resigns as private secretary; installation at Simla; cutting down swagger; religious peace — a Catholic Viceroy who will not play Lytton’s romance.
Chapter XV — The Afghan question (1880)
First six months overshadowed; most of the Hartington correspondence is Afghan. Sher Ali alienated since 1873: Northbrook would not give complete protection; Lytton until the 1877 Peshawar Conference tried to force British agents into the country, then wrote to Cavagnari that the aim was “gradual disintegration and weakening” of Afghan power; Quetta occupied, agent at Gilgit; Sher Ali received a Russian mission. Ripon fences with Abdur Rahman. Maiwand; who was responsible; a strange oversight; politicals vs generals; Roberts’s march to Kandahar.
Chapter XVI — Making the new frontier (1880–1881)
After Kabul is made over to the Amir and Roberts has saved Kandahar, the permanent frontier. Kabul can rest while Abdur Rahman holds (Forward men like Haines regret it). Khyber and Kuram: Roberts’s minute of 29 May wants withdrawal from both if Kandahar is kept and Kuram tribes guaranteed; Stewart concurs; Haines would drop Kuram (Colley’s pet) and hold in front of the Khyber. For and against Kandahar; Pishin as compromise; Council; Ripon has his way; Kandahar evacuated; Cabinet critics; managing the Council.
Chapter XVII — The army and the Russian menace (1881–1884)
Afghan war makes army reform and Central Asian policy actual. Ripon’s views not immediately enforced, later adopted. 1879 Commission on reductions; India Office sits on the report a year, then sends it to India. Ripon had not meant a large army programme; the 1880 campaign changed his mind. With Council (Haines dissenting) he recommends, among other things, abolishing the Commanders-in-Chief of Madras and Bombay. Old fogeys at home; plain words to Gladstone; soldier friends; true defence of India; proposed treaty with Russia; Russia at Merv; Abdur Rahman’s wisdom.
Chapter XVIII — Economic policy (1881–1884)
Serious illness late 1880; he asks Hartington whether a C.S.I. for surgeon Major John Anderson would be “a job” for saving a Viceroy. Illness closes the Afghan-only period. Programme: fiscal reform; land (Famine Commission 1876–77, report 1880); railways; (political, next chapter) Press Act, local self-government, natives in the services. India Office interference; first budget; conflict with Baring; thoughts of resignation; free trade and opium; then friendship with Baring against financial pedants. Zamindars and ryots; Bengal Tenancy Bill; the question in Oudh; Hartington’s appreciation.
Chapter XIX — Political reforms (1882–1884)
If he resisted doctrinaire Radicals on economics, he “avenges” them on politics — still without pedantry. Guiding text: memorandum on local self-government to the Secretary of State, late 1882. Education, a free press, legal for discretionary administration, railways and telegraphs, easier communication with Europe: “we have entered upon a period of change”; public opinion growing; the movement will go faster every year. Scheme as an educative measure (“talking and doing”); bureaucrats; “an unseemly document”; ten years after. Vernacular Press Act repealed (Viceroy’s diplomacy). Education policy; Indians in the Civil Service.
Chapter XX — The Ilbert Bill (1883–1884)
2 October 1882 to Hartington: if you back local self-government, I shall not give much more trouble; 12 October: except education, land-revenue assessment is probably the last great subject. Written after the dispatch proposing the Criminal Procedure Code Amendment Bill — so Ripon did not think Ilbert a great measure. Storm; friends (Hughes, Miss Lyall, Northbrook, Halifax, Plowden) say he has bitten off too much. Origin; Hope’s “crotchet”; official proposals; emotional propaganda; Ripon’s defence; “a great mistake”; Maine’s mislaid minute; no surrender; risk of a row; the Concordat; no sacrifice of principle; noble epilogue.
Chapter XXI — End of the viceroyalty (1884)
After Ilbert, the work is done except minor measures left to Dufferin (Bengal and Oudh tenancy). Ripon had hoped Dufferin would succeed him. Departure advanced: viceroyalty had six months to run, but a government in extremis must not make the appointment if a dissolution comes at the end of 1884; Dufferin named in August, relieves in December. Ripon is not sorry: the work has been telling. Indian love and gratitude; letters of farewell; a self-willed councillor; “epoch-making”; popularity; “fanatic of moderate views.”
Book V — The elder statesman
Chapter XXII — Home Rule and a naval interlude (1885–1892)
He lands 23 January 1885 into Transvaal, Egypt, Sudan, Ireland, and Whig–Radical war in cabinet. Algernon West’s gossip to Lady Ripon; Brett from Hartington’s office; Dilke’s Friday cabinet notes (sixty-four letters, 1880–February 1883). While he travelled: new Reform Act (county franchise, his pet aversion) and Chamberlain’s Ipswich Unauthorized Programme. Home Rule takes embryonic shape. Churchill at the India Office vs Ripon; Gavan Duffy’s plan; on the Nationalist side; Tom Hughes’s anger. Admiralty: a fight for the fleet. Home Rule rejected; Liberal reunion?; embassy to Ireland, enthusiastic welcome; 1892, an embarrassing victory.
Chapter XXIII — Problems of empire (1892–1895)
Days after the election Gladstone is planning a fourth administration; Hawarden, 23 July 1892: Ripon among the first called; Gladstone “fast bound to Ireland as Ulysses was to his mast.” Second Home Rule Bill; Gladstone retires. Ripon and the new imperialism; imperial federation; combining against the Treasury; colonial preferences; a tussle with Cecil Rhodes; Ottawa Conference; Ripon’s historic dispatch; unifying South Africa; Swaziland; Kruger; Boer access to the sea; German danger (“hands off”); entente with France.
Chapter XXIV — Liberal leadership (1895–1905)
After Gladstone (March 1894) the succession is anarchy: Rosebery vs Harcourt. Harcourt has experience and Commons following, is disliked in cabinet; Rosebery is popular, a Peer and Imperialist, anathema to Commons Radicals. Choice falls on Rosebery mainly because a cabinet will not endure Harcourt’s temper. Jameson Raid; Rosebery resigns leadership; Ripon’s remonstrance; no Harcourt leadership; a dual arrangement; Harcourt retires. Boer War; advice to Campbell-Bannerman; party dissensions; Rosebery’s reticence then “speaks out”; rival tabernacles; fight for free trade; C.-B.’s dilemma; Rosebery’s last exit.
Chapter XXV — Last years in office (1905–1908)
January 1906: Liberal majority of 190 over Conservatives, Liberal Unionists, and Nationalists combined. Ripon as Leader in the Lords has a Premier’s scope without a Premier’s ease (departmental colleagues are often beginners). Education Bill 1906: a stout fight. Death of Lady Ripon; he wishes to retire. Morley’s Indian reforms. Foreign politics; Triple Entente. Asquith premier; Lords leadership; final resignation. Grey’s tribute; colleagues’ regrets; Spencer’s message.
Chapter XXVI — Gathered to his people (1909)
Survives office nine months. Health worse; still London, still a vote for Crewe in the Lords; Fitzmaurice on foreign papers; Runciman’s Education Bill (brings Runciman and Archbishop Bourne together). Nearest his heart: Indian Councils Bill still pending; a message to India. Death; last letters; Buxton: statesman and administrator; “as chief, as friend, as colleague.”
